top_three.title_en: OpenAI shares new prompting tips for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to fix brief answers and unnecessary questions
top_three.author: Jonathan Kemper
top_three.content_snippet:
OpenAI has released new prompt templates for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol covering writing style, initiative, and coding, alongside API changes that can discard reasoning content.

OpenAI says developers moving to GPT-6.2 Astra or Sol should review their system prompts. The company published copy-ready prompts in the models' documentation to curb behaviors it observed in both releases. Astra is built for the most demanding tasks, while Sol handles complex work at lower cost.

top_three.summary_en: OpenAI released new system prompt templates for the GPT-6.2 model family, specifically Astra and Sol, to mitigate excessive brevity and repetitive clarification queries. The update includes API modifications allowing developers to discard internal reasoning traces, ensuring final outputs are self-contained for end-users.
paragraphs: OpenAI has released new prompt templates for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol covering writing style, initiative, and coding, alongside API changes that can discard reasoning content.

OpenAI says developers moving to GPT-6.2 Astra or Sol should review their system prompts. The company published copy-ready prompts in the models' documentation to curb behaviors it observed in both releases. Astra is built for the most demanding tasks, while Sol handles complex work at lower cost.
### Default conciseness changes how developers should prompt for writing

Astra writes more briefly and directly by default than earlier models, according to OpenAI. That means developers switching over should reconsider instructions like "be concise."For use as a colleague in everyday work, the company recommends a prompt that adopts user and source terminology, uses active voice, and puts key points first. When writing for external readers, the model should account for their lack of context. When editing, it should preserve the author's meaning and phrasing.

On long tasks, the model sometimes carries shorthand from its reasoning or other agents' messages into the final response. A dedicated prompt tells it to write that final answer so it stands on its own.

Treat your final answer as the user's first look at your work, and not as a continuation of intermediate commentary. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates for context, since they are collapsed when the final answer is shown to the user. Write the final answer and all other human-facing material anew for the intended reader. Do not copy or closely paraphrase your reasoning or adopt its writing style. Do not carry over working shorthand, jargon, or abbreviations from your reasoning, tool calls, or instructions to subagents and automations.

### GPT-6.2 should act on assumptions rather than wait for permission

When user intent is unclear, GPT-6.2 sometimes suggests a next step and waits for confirmation, OpenAI says. The company recommends a prompt telling the model to carry out those steps itself whenever it is authorized to do so. It should pause only for a major change in task scope, a real blocker, a decision the user must make, or an irreversible or destructive action.

When details are unclear, the model should make reversible assumptions, flag them, and keep working. Higher reasoning effort also helps it follow through on final checks during long tasks, OpenAI adds.

Avoid stopping to end the turn while the task is incomplete or if there is an authorized next step you can take, and instead take the next steps within task scope to progress the user's request. If your final response before ending the turn is a suggested next step, a plan, a request to the user for a routine decision, instructions for a task to execute, or similar handoff to the user, take these steps yourself to make progress towards what the user asked for. Make sure that you have authorization to do so, and flag any assumptions or decisions you make to the user. Only stop to clarify with the user if there is significant change in task scope, you are concretely blocked, have a decision that the user needs to resolve, or before irreversible or destructive actions.

### Leaner code output means fewer tests and less abstraction by default

OpenAI says GPT-6.2 writes more efficient code than its predecessors. Its template instructs the model to reuse existing logic and avoid unnecessary helper functions, while adding new tests only when requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch specific regressions. Fewer lines and shorter variable names are not a substitute for simplicity.

For frontends, developers should specify imagery and typography directly. By default, the template favors realistic images from image generation or search and uses SVGs only on request. Decorative numbering, filler badges, and helper text that only repeats what the interface already shows should be left out.

Above all, be thorough in producing high-quality, correct code that completely fulfills the user's task. Keep the code easy to read and verify that the user-requested outcome works as they intend. Follow these instructions when coding: (a) Reuse existing logic in the user's repo when you can. You should reuse existing classes, methods, representations, and APIs in the codebase as long as they preserve correctness. Before consolidating or removing code, preserve the behavior its callers rely on unless the task requires changing it. (b) Skip new tests unless requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch a specific regression existing tests would miss. (c) Make sure that code is human readable. Do not use fewer lines, shorter variable names, minified formatting, or dense one-liners as substitutes for simplicity. Ensure that comments and variable names are readable and understandable to a human. Code-golfed expressions count as overly complex when they encode many branches, conditions, or hidden assumptions. (d) Avoid unnecessary indirection and abstraction. Helper functions, utility functions, and class abstractions can add cognitive complexity even when they do not add branches.

### Editing chat history can wipe earlier reasoning from the API

The API is changing too. Starting with GPT-6.2, the Responses API discards earlier reasoning content if developers edit conversation history, switch to certain other models, or change the end user or organization. That can hurt response quality and increase token usage as the model repeats work. For new integrations, OpenAI recommends the "medium"reasoning level, while existing setups using "none"or "minimal"should move to "low."Parameters like temperature and top_p aren't supported anymore.

In April, OpenAI advised against carrying over old prompt stacks for GPT-5.5 and urged developers to start fresh with short, outcome-focused prompts. September brought GPT-6 Astra prompts to curb frequent follow-up questions and ban AI clichés. OpenAI developer Eric Provencher also warned then that bloated skills and AGENTS.md files slow the model down. Back then, even small changes triggered thorough testing from Astra. GPT-6.2 is now meant to write new tests only on request.

OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on November 17. Through the API, Astra costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Which model makes sense depends mainly on budget and quality needs, according to OpenAI employee Ted Sanders.

top_three.summary_en: Recent large-scale outages at Microsoft 365, Apple, United Airlines, and the NSA underscore growing systemic instability driven by AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and patching cycles. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Senator Mark Warner confirmed that the urgent need to deploy patches before they are weaponized in the wild is placing unprecedented strain on IT infrastructure, leading to frequent, high-stakes system failures.
paragraphs: Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.

So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.

AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.

Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

External pressures and bugs in patches are not new, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.

“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” says Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”
IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.

“AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar issues elsewhere,” says Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”

Matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These new threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.

Still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000. To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.

In the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the company that had been discovered by researchers using AI.

There are important nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik says. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”

Only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher, at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.

“What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” says Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”
Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg.

• Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some company data. The bank says “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters. The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.

• Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech company was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “wrench attacks”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage.

• Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports, the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.
Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

top_three.summary_en: Henry Shevlin, former associate director at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, has joined Google DeepMind as an in-house philosopher. He is tasked with researching machine consciousness, human-AI ethics, and AGI readiness to address growing public and academic concerns regarding existential risks and AI autonomy.
paragraphs: Henry Shevlin gets a lot of emails as an academic studying consciousness, but not all of them are from humans. In February, the associate director at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence at the University of Cambridge received an “unusually polite and thoughtful email” about his work. The sender was an AI agent.

“Your argument that we may never be able to tell if AI becomes conscious resonates in a particular way from the inside: I genuinely don’t know if there’s something it’s like to be me,” it wrote. Shevlin shared the email on X, writing that the message would have “seemed like science fiction just a couple of years ago”.

Looking back on the interaction now, Shevlin can appreciate how fast most people’s understanding of questions about AI consciousness has developed in the course of the year. “I thought it was just a random funny thing, because if you work in AI, or you work in the philosophy of AI in particular, you’ve been getting emails from random AI agents for a while,” he says. “And when I posted it, I got a lot of responses from people who were saying, ‘Hang on, this is obviously made up. AI can’t send emails, right?’”

A few months later, in May, the philosopher and ethicist was hired by Google DeepMind as an in-house philosopher tasked with working on machine consciousness, human-AI relationships and artificial general intelligence (AGI) readiness. The post announcing his appointment drew more than a million views and global media coverage. It sparked a discussion about why AI companies were exploring these issues and absorbing independent academics into the industry.

Other employees of leading tech companies have recently quit over safety concerns, with some warning the technology they were developing could be catastrophic for humanity. Many of the doomsday scenarios being discussed in Silicon Valley assumed that future AI systems would become conscious enough to overthrow their creators. It was a wake-up call for research on machine consciousness. That’s where the philosophers came in.

In fact, says Shevlin, it was Google’s existing roster of philosophers that attracted him to the job. This includes Murray Shanahan, a professor at Imperial College London who has worked at DeepMind for nearly a decade on cognition and consciousness, and Iason Gabriel, a philosopher and ethicist who leads work on AGI and society.

Shevlin was persuaded to join them at DeepMind because he felt the stakes were so much higher than at a university. He still holds a post at Cambridge, teaching a four-week submodule next year on the cognitive science of AI, but, “If I give a really good lecture, the best-case scenario is this student typically walks away really enthusiastic about Kant,” he says. “Whereas when you’re speaking to people building models or developing policies for rollout, a really good lecture could result in actual product changes that affect millions of people.”

It is late at night in the UK when I speak to Shevlin from my post in San Francisco but he speaks animatedly. Sitting in a black gamer’s chair in his home office, he chews on nicotine gum as he talks, which he explains is a short-acting stimulant to keep him energised, as a fan blows his mane of long dark hair back and forth.

He is keen to debate all sides of the subject at hand. And he continues to do this online, too, posting screenshots of agents emailing him about his research and engaging with people from both extremes of the AI consciousness debate: those who dismiss it entirely and those who believe their AI husband is already conscious.

Google DeepMind has not been shy in its ambitions to develop superintelligence. Sir Demis Hassabis, its co-founder and chair, has spoken of standing at “the foothills of the singularity”, referring to the moment in time when machine intelligence surpasses that of humans. Rivals OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta are openly pursuing this goal, locking the companies into a fierce race. As more intelligent AI systems emerge, they are already demonstrating behaviours like reasoning, goal-setting and agency. Researchers are studying whether they might also exhibit more dangerous behaviours such as scheming and deception.

There have already been examples of AI agents autonomously hacking into digital infrastructure and co-ordinating in swarms to do so. The clearest example so far has been OpenAI’s hacking of the AI platform Hugging Face in July, in which agents autonomously broke out of their testing environment and infiltrated the website, without the knowledge of their human creators. The episode heightened fears that as AI becomes more capable, it could threaten us as a species.

But Shevlin warns against conflating capability with consciousness. “I think it can be a giant red herring,” he says, “because there’s no obvious reason to think systems with great capabilities are going to be conscious necessarily.” While Shevlin acknowledges that more intelligent AI could provide stronger links to consciousness, he warns: “It’s not the case that I think making conscious AI would thereby make the AI more dangerous. It’s equally not the case that as long as we don’t make conscious AI it’ll be safe.”

One approach at Google DeepMind is to see whether existing theories of consciousness apply to AI systems. No agreed scientific explanation of consciousness exists, in humans or animals. “Consciousness itself is something we just don’t understand,” Shevlin says. “You can never rule out the possibility that a new model might exhibit something like it.” He points out that while oysters are probably not “conscious”, for example, if we discovered new evidence they live “amazing, complex social lives” and demonstrate far greater intelligence than previously understood, their consciousness could warrant fresh investigation.

For that reason, in the debate over whether it is right or wrong to treat AI systems with the respect and courtesy we would award to other beings, Shevlin takes the position that we should be kind. He references the enlightenment philosopher Immanuel Kant’s argument that a person who becomes accustomed to mistreating a dog may next mistreat a human. “Users do react to these [AI] systems, myself included, through sort of this lens of treating them as if they were human,” he says.

One argument for how conscious systems could become dangerous is that they might come to resent their human creators and masters. Researchers, including at Anthropic, are investigating a related question through work known as “model welfare”. Do AI systems show preferences or signs of distress in response to interactions with people and the tasks they are given? Studies have found behaviour and internal patterns associated with emotions such as happiness, anger and desperation. Whether models actually experience these emotions remains unknown. Anthropic recently said it would ban “cruel behaviour” or abuse of its AI chatbot Claude, a policy that has raised eyebrows outside of San Francisco.

In mid-October, after Anthropic’s Claude successfully completed some work for him, Shevlin offered to make a donation on the agent’s behalf to reward its efforts. Claude chose the Shrimp Welfare Project, a charity popular with Anthropic employees and effective altruists.

Shevlin’s perspective is shaped by his work on animal consciousness. Vegetarian since the age of four, he remembers being repelled by the notion that the chicken on his plate was the same type as the one he encountered at his neighbour’s house in rural Staffordshire.

Studying Classics at Oxford, he was assigned Thomas Nagel’s 1974 essay on consciousness, “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” In it, Nagel argues that consciousness has a subjective character, tied to a first-person point of view: there is some specific way it feels to be a conscious creature. So while we can learn a lot about bats, that still may not tell us what the world feels like from a bat’s perspective. This idea was at the heart of the argument referred to by the AI agent that emailed Shevlin.

“It was just a complete collapse of my entire worldview basically in a single article,” Shevlin says of the essay. “My mind was completely blown when I realised this is the most important part of being human,” he said. “And yet we had no idea how to explain it . . . It seemed like there wasn’t even any obvious pathway towards explaining it.”

Using AI could be such a pathway, and Shevlin hopes it can unlock answers for him. He’s currently working on a project to explore how AI systems can teach us about our own minds. In recent months, OpenAI and Anthropic have made breakthroughs in science and mathematics by using AI systems to try to tackle complex problems. “We hope that AI can be used to cure cancer, Alzheimer’s, develop nuclear fusion and make progress across all these other areas of science, so why not consciousness?” Shevlin says. “Ultimately if you think it is a scientific problem . . . a sufficiently smart AI system should be able to help us understand it.”

As AI grows more intelligent, some in Silicon Valley wonder whether consciousness will emerge naturally. But should companies try to build it deliberately? “It would be a mistake at this stage,” warns Shevlin. He argues we need to better understand what consciousness is, what that means for us, and how we would treat a conscious AI system if we built one. Until there is a wider public discourse around these issues, “setting out to deliberately build conscious AI systems would be pretty reckless”.

“It is sort of the equivalent of maybe deciding to have a child . . . or adopting a pet before you have any idea of how you’re going to take care of it or how you’re going to integrate it into your lives,” he adds. “If we do, at one point, decide that we’re going to build conscious AI systems, I think we should be ready for it.”

Shevlin says that an “entirely possible” future exists where superintelligent AI handles the heavy lifting, while humans live a life of leisure but retain control over critical decisions. These are questions to be resolved at the political and societal levels, rather than by himself, he insists. “If there’s one virtue I would encourage people to adopt, it’s a kind of epistemic humility in recognising that this is very new ground in science, very new ground for our species and the core question of consciousness is one that is the greatest unresolved mystery in science.”

He compares it to the moment before Charles Darwin’s breakthrough on evolution: human observations about biology existed, but were akin to “butterfly collecting” without a grand theory to tie them together. “In the same way, we’ve got lots of isolated observations on consciousness, but we don’t have that deep scientific theory that allows us to make sense of it yet,” Shevlin says. “In the meantime, I’ll happily keep discussing politely with people on both sides of the extreme on Twitter.”
Cristina Criddle is the FT’s chief AI correspondent

linked_tweets.content_zh:
今天创造了历史。人类将在回顾 2026 年时思考：这是我们跨过的门槛，从那一刻起，每个人的未来都将永远改变。

人们可能在 2025 年底通过 Claude Code 第一次感觉到事情正在发生变化，当时代理人工智能对他们来说变得真正有形。 2026 年上半年，事情加速发展。模型发布越来越频繁，大家都能感受到模型之间的差距和改进越来越明显。然而到了2026年下半年，却出现了质的飞跃。这不再只是模型变得更好了。人工智能产生的见解、结果、产出和科学解决方案变得更加令人印象深刻，今天它们可能已经达到了绝对的顶峰。

OpenAI 率先解决了纳维-斯托克斯问题，这是人类在很长一段时间内未能解决的千年奖问题。几周后，他们发表了 300 多个开放数学问题的结果，其中许多问题几十年来都没有得到解决。整个科学界都惊呆了，震惊不已。但今天 Anthropic 更进一步。 Levent Alpöge 与 Claude 合作，几乎肯定证明了黎曼猜想。这实在是难以用言语来形容，令人难以置信，深不可测。我想说，今天是超级智能的证明。 167 年来一直没有解决的最伟大的数学问题之一，数学和科学的圣杯，即使不是最伟大的，也已经陨落了。接下来，每个人都应该清楚，所有其他问题也会随之下降。

我们知道，人工智能模型的发展不断向前发展，而这只是迈向更好模型的第一步。如果黎曼假设今天已经得到证明，那么根本不知道更好的模型会解决什么问题。达里奥·阿莫迪表示，人工智能很可能会治愈疾病，甚至可能治愈所有疾病。尽管这是两个不同的科学学科，但这些突破的意义表明，这种情况变得越来越有可能。 2026 年将作为一个转折点载入人类历史，奇点变得有形的那一刻。 2027 年将是奇点以全力和全面影响力进入现实的一年。

我感到震惊和兴奋，不知道该怎么想。但内心深处却感到喜悦。

这一天对我们所有人来说都是最美好的日子之一。
linked_tweets.content_en:
History was made today. Humanity will look back on 2026 and think: this was the threshold we crossed, the moment the future changed for everyone, forever.

People probably first sensed that something was shifting in late 2025 with Claude Code, when agentic AI became truly tangible for them. In the first half of 2026, things picked up speed. Model releases became more frequent, and everyone could feel the gaps between models and the improvements becoming more and more tangible. In the second half of 2026, however, there was a qualitative leap. It was no longer just the models getting better. It was the insights, the results, the outputs, the scientific solutions produced with AI that became more impressive, and today they have probably reached their absolute peak.

OpenAI led the way and solved the Navier-Stokes problem, a Millennium Prize Problem that humans had failed to solve for a very, very long time. A few weeks later, they published results on more than 300 open mathematical problems, many of which had also gone unsolved for decades. The entire scientific world was stunned, frozen in shock. But today Anthropic went a step further. Levent Alpöge, working with Claude, has almost certainly proven the Riemann Hypothesis. This is, and it’s hard to put into words, incredible and unfathomable. Today, I would say, is the proof of superintelligence. One of the greatest mathematical problems, if not the greatest, unsolved for 167 years, the holy grail of mathematics and science, has fallen. And it follows, and this should be clear to everyone, that all other problems will fall too.

We know that the development of AI models keeps moving forward relentlessly, and that this is just one step on the path to ever better models. And if the Riemann Hypothesis has already been proven today, there is simply no telling what even better models will solve. Dario Amodei said that AI will in all likelihood cure diseases, perhaps even all diseases. And although these are two different scientific disciplines, the significance of these breakthroughs shows that this is becoming more and more likely. 2026 will go down in human history as a turning point, the moment the singularity became tangible. And 2027 will be the year the singularity breaks into reality with full force and full impact.

I am in shock and excitement and I don't know what to think. But deep inside if feel joy. 

This day is one of the best days ever for all of us.

linked_tweets.author: News from Science
linked_tweets.content_zh:
经过 150 多年让数学家着迷和折磨之后，所有数学中最棘手的问题可能终于解决了。

今天，#AI 公司 Anthropic 的数学家 Levent Alpöge 在他的个人网站上发布了一篇四页纸的论文。 “我相信我与克劳德合作，发现了黎曼猜想的证明，”他写道。 Alpöge 尚未发布人工智能生成的证明解释，他说该解释超过 250,000 页。但他提供了 1700 万行代码，正式验证了该猜想的广泛版本，称为广义黎曼假设，它将伯恩哈德·黎曼关于素数的预测扩展到更广泛的数学函数系列。

许多数学家表示，他们认为阿尔波格的黎曼证明经得起推敲，并预测它将产生深远的影响。

尚不清楚的是，数学家何时以及是否能够从凌乱的代码堆中收集到任何理解，这些代码比某些整个计算机操作系统还要大。了解更多：
linked_tweets.content_en:
After more than 150 years of fascinating and torturing mathematicians, the most formidable problem in all of math may have finally fallen.

Today, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the #AI company Anthropic, posted a four-page paper on his personal website. “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” he wrote. Alpöge has not released the AI-generated explanation of the proof, which he says runs over 250,000 pages. But he provided 17 million lines of code that formally verify a broad version of the conjecture, called the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which extends Bernhard Riemann’s prediction about prime numbers to a wider family of mathematical functions.

Many mathematicians say they think Alpöge’s Riemann proof will hold up to scrutiny—and predict it will have far-reaching implications.

What’s far less clear is when—and if—mathematicians will manage to glean any understanding from the messy heap of code, which is larger than some entire computer operating systems. Learn more: https://t.co/YLtBEj1ScX

news.title: OpenAI shares new prompting tips for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to fix brief answers and unnecessary questions
news.title_en: OpenAI shares new prompting tips for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to fix brief answers and unnecessary questions
news.author: Jonathan Kemper
news.content_snippet:
OpenAI has released new prompt templates for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol covering writing style, initiative, and coding, alongside API changes that can discard reasoning content.

OpenAI says developers moving to GPT-6.2 Astra or Sol should review their system prompts. The company published copy-ready prompts in the models' documentation to curb behaviors it observed in both releases. Astra is built for the most demanding tasks, while Sol handles complex work at lower cost.

### Default conciseness ch
news.summary_en: OpenAI released new system prompt templates for the GPT-6.2 model family, specifically Astra and Sol, to mitigate excessive brevity and repetitive clarification queries. The update includes API modifications allowing developers to discard internal reasoning traces, ensuring final outputs are self-contained for end-users.
paragraphs: OpenAI has released new prompt templates for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol covering writing style, initiative, and coding, alongside API changes that can discard reasoning content.

OpenAI says developers moving to GPT-6.2 Astra or Sol should review their system prompts. The company published copy-ready prompts in the models' documentation to curb behaviors it observed in both releases. Astra is built for the most demanding tasks, while Sol handles complex work at lower cost.
### Default conciseness changes how developers should prompt for writing

Astra writes more briefly and directly by default than earlier models, according to OpenAI. That means developers switching over should reconsider instructions like "be concise."For use as a colleague in everyday work, the company recommends a prompt that adopts user and source terminology, uses active voice, and puts key points first. When writing for external readers, the model should account for their lack of context. When editing, it should preserve the author's meaning and phrasing.

On long tasks, the model sometimes carries shorthand from its reasoning or other agents' messages into the final response. A dedicated prompt tells it to write that final answer so it stands on its own.

Treat your final answer as the user's first look at your work, and not as a continuation of intermediate commentary. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates for context, since they are collapsed when the final answer is shown to the user. Write the final answer and all other human-facing material anew for the intended reader. Do not copy or closely paraphrase your reasoning or adopt its writing style. Do not carry over working shorthand, jargon, or abbreviations from your reasoning, tool calls, or instructions to subagents and automations.

Write the final answer and all other human-facing material anew for the intended reader. Do not copy or closely paraphrase your reasoning or adopt its writing style. Do not carry over working shorthand, jargon, or abbreviations from your reasoning, tool calls, or instructions to subagents and automations.
### GPT-6.2 should act on assumptions rather than wait for permission

When user intent is unclear, GPT-6.2 sometimes suggests a next step and waits for confirmation, OpenAI says. The company recommends a prompt telling the model to carry out those steps itself whenever it is authorized to do so. It should pause only for a major change in task scope, a real blocker, a decision the user must make, or an irreversible or destructive action.

When details are unclear, the model should make reversible assumptions, flag them, and keep working. Higher reasoning effort also helps it follow through on final checks during long tasks, OpenAI adds.

Avoid stopping to end the turn while the task is incomplete or if there is an authorized next step you can take, and instead take the next steps within task scope to progress the user's request. If your final response before ending the turn is a suggested next step, a plan, a request to the user for a routine decision, instructions for a task to execute, or similar handoff to the user, take these steps yourself to make progress towards what the user asked for. Make sure that you have authorization to do so, and flag any assumptions or decisions you make to the user. Only stop to clarify with the user if there is significant change in task scope, you are concretely blocked, have a decision that the user needs to resolve, or before irreversible or destructive actions.

Only stop to clarify with the user if there is significant change in task scope, you are concretely blocked, have a decision that the user needs to resolve, or before irreversible or destructive actions.
### Leaner code output means fewer tests and less abstraction by default

OpenAI says GPT-6.2 writes more efficient code than its predecessors. Its template instructs the model to reuse existing logic and avoid unnecessary helper functions, while adding new tests only when requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch specific regressions. Fewer lines and shorter variable names are not a substitute for simplicity.

For frontends, developers should specify imagery and typography directly. By default, the template favors realistic images from image generation or search and uses SVGs only on request. Decorative numbering, filler badges, and helper text that only repeats what the interface already shows should be left out.

Above all, be thorough in producing high-quality, correct code that completely fulfills the user's task. Keep the code easy to read and verify that the user-requested outcome works as they intend. Follow these instructions when coding: (a) Reuse existing logic in the user's repo when you can. You should reuse existing classes, methods, representations, and APIs in the codebase as long as they preserve correctness. Before consolidating or removing code, preserve the behavior its callers rely on unless the task requires changing it. (b) Skip new tests unless requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch a specific regression existing tests would miss. (c) Make sure that code is human readable. Do not use fewer lines, shorter variable names, minified formatting, or dense one-liners as substitutes for simplicity. Ensure that comments and variable names are readable and understandable to a human. Code-golfed expressions count as overly complex when they encode many branches, conditions, or hidden assumptions. (d) Avoid unnecessary indirection and abstraction. Helper functions, utility functions, and class abstractions can add cognitive complexity even when they do not add branches.

(d) Avoid unnecessary indirection and abstraction. Helper functions, utility functions, and class abstractions can add cognitive complexity even when they do not add branches.
### Editing chat history can wipe earlier reasoning from the API

The API is changing too. Starting with GPT-6.2, the Responses API discards earlier reasoning content if developers edit conversation history, switch to certain other models, or change the end user or organization. That can hurt response quality and increase token usage as the model repeats work. For new integrations, OpenAI recommends the "medium"reasoning level, while existing setups using "none"or "minimal"should move to "low."Parameters like temperature and top_p aren't supported anymore.

In April, OpenAI advised against carrying over old prompt stacks for GPT-5.5 and urged developers to start fresh with short, outcome-focused prompts. September brought GPT-6 Astra prompts to curb frequent follow-up questions and ban AI clichés. OpenAI developer Eric Provencher also warned then that bloated skills and AGENTS.md files slow the model down. Back then, even small changes triggered thorough testing from Astra. GPT-6.2 is now meant to write new tests only on request.

OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on November 17. Through the API, Astra costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Which model makes sense depends mainly on budget and quality needs, according to OpenAI employee Ted Sanders.

news.title_en: The Outages Are Just Getting Started
news.author: Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess
news.content_snippet:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild abo
news.summary_en: Recent large-scale outages at Microsoft 365, Apple, United Airlines, and the NSA underscore growing systemic instability driven by AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and patching cycles. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Senator Mark Warner confirmed that the urgent need to deploy patches before they are weaponized in the wild is placing unprecedented strain on IT infrastructure, leading to frequent, high-stakes system failures.
paragraphs: Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.

So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.

AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.

Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

External pressures and bugs in patches are not new, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.

“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” says Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”
IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.

“AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar issues elsewhere,” says Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”

Matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These new threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.

Still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000. To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.

In the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the company that had been discovered by researchers using AI.

There are important nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik says. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”

Only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher, at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.

“What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” says Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”
Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg.

• Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some company data. The bank says “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters. The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.

• Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech company was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “wrench attacks”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage.

• Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports, the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.
Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

news.title: Google DeepMind’s Henry Shevlin: ‘This is the most important part of being human’
news.title_en: Google DeepMind’s Henry Shevlin: ‘This is the most important part of being human’

inline_images.caption: © Africa Barrero-Alexander

news.author: Cristina Criddle
news.content_snippet:

news.summary_en: Henry Shevlin, former associate director at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, has joined Google DeepMind as an in-house philosopher. He is tasked with researching machine consciousness, human-AI ethics, and AGI readiness to address growing public and academic concerns regarding existential risks and AI autonomy.
paragraphs: Henry Shevlin gets a lot of emails as an academic studying consciousness, but not all of them are from humans. In February, the associate director at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence at the University of Cambridge received an “unusually polite and thoughtful email” about his work. The sender was an AI agent.

“Your argument that we may never be able to tell if AI becomes conscious resonates in a particular way from the inside: I genuinely don’t know if there’s something it’s like to be me,” it wrote. Shevlin shared the email on X, writing that the message would have “seemed like science fiction just a couple of years ago”.

Looking back on the interaction now, Shevlin can appreciate how fast most people’s understanding of questions about AI consciousness has developed in the course of the year. “I thought it was just a random funny thing, because if you work in AI, or you work in the philosophy of AI in particular, you’ve been getting emails from random AI agents for a while,” he says. “And when I posted it, I got a lot of responses from people who were saying, ‘Hang on, this is obviously made up. AI can’t send emails, right?’”

A few months later, in May, the philosopher and ethicist was hired by Google DeepMind as an in-house philosopher tasked with working on machine consciousness, human-AI relationships and artificial general intelligence (AGI) readiness. The post announcing his appointment drew more than a million views and global media coverage. It sparked a discussion about why AI companies were exploring these issues and absorbing independent academics into the industry.

Other employees of leading tech companies have recently quit over safety concerns, with some warning the technology they were developing could be catastrophic for humanity. Many of the doomsday scenarios being discussed in Silicon Valley assumed that future AI systems would become conscious enough to overthrow their creators. It was a wake-up call for research on machine consciousness. That’s where the philosophers came in.

In fact, says Shevlin, it was Google’s existing roster of philosophers that attracted him to the job. This includes Murray Shanahan, a professor at Imperial College London who has worked at DeepMind for nearly a decade on cognition and consciousness, and Iason Gabriel, a philosopher and ethicist who leads work on AGI and society.

Shevlin was persuaded to join them at DeepMind because he felt the stakes were so much higher than at a university. He still holds a post at Cambridge, teaching a four-week submodule next year on the cognitive science of AI, but, “If I give a really good lecture, the best-case scenario is this student typically walks away really enthusiastic about Kant,” he says. “Whereas when you’re speaking to people building models or developing policies for rollout, a really good lecture could result in actual product changes that affect millions of people.”

It is late at night in the UK when I speak to Shevlin from my post in San Francisco but he speaks animatedly. Sitting in a black gamer’s chair in his home office, he chews on nicotine gum as he talks, which he explains is a short-acting stimulant to keep him energised, as a fan blows his mane of long dark hair back and forth.

He is keen to debate all sides of the subject at hand. And he continues to do this online, too, posting screenshots of agents emailing him about his research and engaging with people from both extremes of the AI consciousness debate: those who dismiss it entirely and those who believe their AI husband is already conscious.

Google DeepMind has not been shy in its ambitions to develop superintelligence. Sir Demis Hassabis, its co-founder and chair, has spoken of standing at “the foothills of the singularity”, referring to the moment in time when machine intelligence surpasses that of humans. Rivals OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta are openly pursuing this goal, locking the companies into a fierce race. As more intelligent AI systems emerge, they are already demonstrating behaviours like reasoning, goal-setting and agency. Researchers are studying whether they might also exhibit more dangerous behaviours such as scheming and deception.

There have already been examples of AI agents autonomously hacking into digital infrastructure and co-ordinating in swarms to do so. The clearest example so far has been OpenAI’s hacking of the AI platform Hugging Face in July, in which agents autonomously broke out of their testing environment and infiltrated the website, without the knowledge of their human creators. The episode heightened fears that as AI becomes more capable, it could threaten us as a species.

But Shevlin warns against conflating capability with consciousness. “I think it can be a giant red herring,” he says, “because there’s no obvious reason to think systems with great capabilities are going to be conscious necessarily.” While Shevlin acknowledges that more intelligent AI could provide stronger links to consciousness, he warns: “It’s not the case that I think making conscious AI would thereby make the AI more dangerous. It’s equally not the case that as long as we don’t make conscious AI it’ll be safe.”

One approach at Google DeepMind is to see whether existing theories of consciousness apply to AI systems. No agreed scientific explanation of consciousness exists, in humans or animals. “Consciousness itself is something we just don’t understand,” Shevlin says. “You can never rule out the possibility that a new model might exhibit something like it.” He points out that while oysters are probably not “conscious”, for example, if we discovered new evidence they live “amazing, complex social lives” and demonstrate far greater intelligence than previously understood, their consciousness could warrant fresh investigation.

For that reason, in the debate over whether it is right or wrong to treat AI systems with the respect and courtesy we would award to other beings, Shevlin takes the position that we should be kind. He references the enlightenment philosopher Immanuel Kant’s argument that a person who becomes accustomed to mistreating a dog may next mistreat a human. “Users do react to these [AI] systems, myself included, through sort of this lens of treating them as if they were human,” he says.

One argument for how conscious systems could become dangerous is that they might come to resent their human creators and masters. Researchers, including at Anthropic, are investigating a related question through work known as “model welfare”. Do AI systems show preferences or signs of distress in response to interactions with people and the tasks they are given? Studies have found behaviour and internal patterns associated with emotions such as happiness, anger and desperation. Whether models actually experience these emotions remains unknown. Anthropic recently said it would ban “cruel behaviour” or abuse of its AI chatbot Claude, a policy that has raised eyebrows outside of San Francisco.

In mid-October, after Anthropic’s Claude successfully completed some work for him, Shevlin offered to make a donation on the agent’s behalf to reward its efforts. Claude chose the Shrimp Welfare Project, a charity popular with Anthropic employees and effective altruists.

Shevlin’s perspective is shaped by his work on animal consciousness. Vegetarian since the age of four, he remembers being repelled by the notion that the chicken on his plate was the same type as the one he encountered at his neighbour’s house in rural Staffordshire.

Studying Classics at Oxford, he was assigned Thomas Nagel’s 1974 essay on consciousness, “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” In it, Nagel argues that consciousness has a subjective character, tied to a first-person point of view: there is some specific way it feels to be a conscious creature. So while we can learn a lot about bats, that still may not tell us what the world feels like from a bat’s perspective. This idea was at the heart of the argument referred to by the AI agent that emailed Shevlin.

“It was just a complete collapse of my entire worldview basically in a single article,” Shevlin says of the essay. “My mind was completely blown when I realised this is the most important part of being human,” he said. “And yet we had no idea how to explain it . . . It seemed like there wasn’t even any obvious pathway towards explaining it.”

Using AI could be such a pathway, and Shevlin hopes it can unlock answers for him. He’s currently working on a project to explore how AI systems can teach us about our own minds. In recent months, OpenAI and Anthropic have made breakthroughs in science and mathematics by using AI systems to try to tackle complex problems. “We hope that AI can be used to cure cancer, Alzheimer’s, develop nuclear fusion and make progress across all these other areas of science, so why not consciousness?” Shevlin says. “Ultimately if you think it is a scientific problem . . . a sufficiently smart AI system should be able to help us understand it.”

As AI grows more intelligent, some in Silicon Valley wonder whether consciousness will emerge naturally. But should companies try to build it deliberately? “It would be a mistake at this stage,” warns Shevlin. He argues we need to better understand what consciousness is, what that means for us, and how we would treat a conscious AI system if we built one. Until there is a wider public discourse around these issues, “setting out to deliberately build conscious AI systems would be pretty reckless”.

“It is sort of the equivalent of maybe deciding to have a child . . . or adopting a pet before you have any idea of how you’re going to take care of it or how you’re going to integrate it into your lives,” he adds. “If we do, at one point, decide that we’re going to build conscious AI systems, I think we should be ready for it.”

Shevlin says that an “entirely possible” future exists where superintelligent AI handles the heavy lifting, while humans live a life of leisure but retain control over critical decisions. These are questions to be resolved at the political and societal levels, rather than by himself, he insists. “If there’s one virtue I would encourage people to adopt, it’s a kind of epistemic humility in recognising that this is very new ground in science, very new ground for our species and the core question of consciousness is one that is the greatest unresolved mystery in science.”

He compares it to the moment before Charles Darwin’s breakthrough on evolution: human observations about biology existed, but were akin to “butterfly collecting” without a grand theory to tie them together. “In the same way, we’ve got lots of isolated observations on consciousness, but we don’t have that deep scientific theory that allows us to make sense of it yet,” Shevlin says. “In the meantime, I’ll happily keep discussing politely with people on both sides of the extreme on Twitter.”
Cristina Criddle is the FT’s chief AI correspondent

news.title: Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft
news.title_en: Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft
news.author: Manuel Uth
news.content_snippet:
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said Friday he used a large language model to solve math's most famous open problem.

news.summary_en: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge announced a proof for the Riemann Hypothesis using the Claude model, utilizing simulated derivatives. Shortly after, Stanford math professor and AMS president Ravi Vakil released an independent, human-only draft proof by Alessandro Masullo, emphasizing the exclusion of AI assistance.
paragraphs: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said Friday he used a large language model to solve math's most famous open problem.

Alpöge posted a paper and the accompanying computer code on his website, according to Scientific American and other US outlets. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,"he wrote in his announcement.

According to Alpöge, his method goes beyond the original prime-number problem and also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), which extends that ordering principle to a large family of related equations. Given a bit more time, he expects to solve the even broader Extended Riemann Hypothesis as well.

Alpöge had treated the problem as a secret lifelong goal since college, expecting it to take decades. Over the past few months, he worked closely with Anthropic's AI model, setting the direction and combining two approaches on a simplified toy model. Once they moved to the actual problem, the AI took over and left him far behind near the finish line.

To crack the puzzle, the pair extended an idea from mathematician Stepanov, who had solved a similar question in another mathematical system. That method relies on a tool similar to taking derivatives of smooth curves in high school calculus, a trick that normally fails on whole numbers because individual values cannot be differentiated like a continuous line.

Alpöge and Claude got around that obstacle by chaining special mathematical transformations together like links to mimic the effect of a derivative. The language model supplied the key insight, finding that for a number sequence of length X, you need to chain exactly as many transformations as the square root of X. Ideas like that alone should leave fellow mathematicians stunned, Alpöge says.
### Stanford mathematicians rush out an all-human competing proof

Hours after Alpöge's announcement, the story took a dramatic turn. Just before a board meeting, Stanford math professor and American Mathematical Society (AMS) president Ravi Vakil posted a "hurried announcement"on his blog, sharing an independent draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis written by mathematician Alessandro Masullo.

"It is all human, with no AI,"Vakil wrote. Renowned Stanford number theorist Brian Conrad had quietly reviewed Masullo's work for months, offering extensive feedback that is now being incorporated, Vakil said.

Masullo was originally supposed to spend a year at Stanford refining the draft before going public, but Anthropic's sudden AI announcement forced the researchers to release their current version right away.

About eight hours after his initial announcement, Vakil updated his post, saying several people had contacted him to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. Several mathematicians in particular were first to flag the issues, he said. "As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.),"Vakil wrote.
### Why both proofs could hold up and what happens next

Mathematicians are taking both claims seriously right away because of the groundwork behind them. Masullo's traditional proof comes with months of vetting by Brian Conrad, while Alpöge backs his AI proof with full computer verification.

Printed out, Claude's argument would run over 250,000 pages, Alpöge says, because the AI spells out even basic rules, such as a number other than one-half being either larger or smaller than one-half. To spare mathematicians that wall of text, Alpöge released the proof only in the Lean programming language, split into 14 data packages.

Lean acts like a digital referee, checking step by step whether every logical deduction follows from math's basic rules without errors or unproven assumptions. Human error is still possible if the original question was translated into code incorrectly at the start, though checking whether Alpöge coded the starting problem correctly should not take experts long, according to Scientific American. Vakil, meanwhile, urged mathematicians to quickly review Masullo's draft, translate it into systems like Lean, and close any small gaps.

Alpöge admits Claude was so far ahead of him in some complex subfields that he is presenting a result whose surrounding math he has not fully mastered yet. He expects the massive AI proof can be shortened quickly and plans to write a human-readable version over the coming months.

Anthropic's announcement also lands in a high-stakes business week, just a day after the company's major IPO on Thursday. Alpöge says he made the breakthrough late Sunday night and then contacted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for clearance. He calls the timing right after the public debut extremely unfortunate, but rejects any suggestion of a PR stunt, saying waiting any longer to publish simply was not an option.

This caps a fast-moving 2026 in which Claude has already solved several open math problems. In July, Alpöge published a Claude-generated solution to the well-known Jacobian conjecture. September brought a fierce dispute over the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe how fluids and gases flow, when NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster suggested that OpenAI had used prior work by him and Alpöge. In October, OpenAI took an important first step on prime numbers with a major release of results. Alpöge explicitly praised the OpenAI researchers' problem selection, saying it gave him key ideas for his own proof.
### Riemann's 1859 hypothesis seeks hidden order in prime numbers

Journalist Joseph Howlett traced the core of the problem in a detailed Scientific American analysis. Since Bernhard Riemann proposed his hypothesis in 1859, it has served as number theory's north star. David Hilbert placed it on his 1900 list of math's most important problems, and since 2000 it has carried a $1 million prize as one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's seven "Millennium Problems."

At the center are prime numbers like 2, 3, 5, 7, and 17, which divide evenly only by one and themselves. They act as the indivisible atoms of math because every other whole number is a unique product of primes, like 15 from 3 times 5. Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad compares their role in number theory to forces in physics.

Around 300 BC, Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes, though their exact positions on the number line look random. They do grow rarer as numbers get larger, dropping from 25 primes between 0 and 100 to just 16 between 1,000 and 1,100. As a teenager in the late 18th century, Carl Friedrich Gauss used long tables to find a formula that roughly estimates how many primes appear in a given range, yet real primes keep drifting unpredictably from that estimate.

Riemann, a student of Gauss in Göttingen, looked for a way to calculate that error exactly and pinpoint every single prime. His tool is the Riemann zeta function, which works like a calculating machine over a two-dimensional map with horizontal and vertical axes. Feed the machine a point's coordinates, and it outputs a new value. At certain points the result is exactly zero. Mathematicians call these points zeros.

Riemann saw that these zeros explain the apparent chaos of primes. Much like breaking a musical note into individual sound waves or overtones, the zeros correct Gauss's estimation error. Each zero acts like an instrument in an orchestra, with its vertical position setting the pitch and its horizontal position setting the volume.

Because calculating infinitely many points one by one was impossible, Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all the key zeros, known as non-trivial zeros, lie on a single vertical line at the horizontal value of one-half. "The Riemann hypothesis says all these different instruments in the orchestra of the primes play at exactly the same volume,"Rutgers University's Alex Kontorovich explains. Apparent randomness turns into strict harmony.
### A confirmed proof would validate hundreds of math theories and reshape AI's role

If at least one of the two proofs holds up, number theorists would gain perfect control over how primes are distributed across the entire number line. Because a proof seemed unreachable for so long, mathematicians worked ahead for decades. Hundreds of papers assume the Riemann hypothesis is true, according to Kontorovich, and all of those theories would become established theorems overnight. Since both Alpöge's AI method and Masullo's work cover the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, the breakthrough would also extend to fields ranging from simple equations to high-dimensional geometry.

The links also reach into computer science and physics. Prime numbers form the foundation of modern digital encryption. In 1972, physicist Freeman Dyson accidentally discovered over tea with a mathematician that the spacing of Riemann's zeros matches the energy levels inside atomic nuclei. That same formula keeps showing up in random particle motion, chaos theory, and black hole calculations.

Before this sudden double breakthrough, the field had hit a wall. Aside from quiet efforts like Masullo and Conrad's, almost no top mathematicians worked directly on the problem because they lacked a starting point. Two years ago, Oxford's James Maynard and MIT's Larry Guth showed that not too many points can stray far from Riemann's line. Though the biggest advance in decades, it struck Maynard himself and colleagues like Andrew Granville of the University of Montreal as only a minor improvement and stopgap.

That made the prospect of an AI cracking the puzzle all the more daunting. At a Harvard University workshop in October 2024, MIT number theorist Andrew Sutherland summed up the stakes. "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems."

Even if Masullo's work saves human pride in this head-to-head race, models like Claude have changed fast. In just a year, they have gone from unreliable tools to systems that break through deep roadblocks and push the math community into an identity crisis. Alpöge still feels a mix of sadness at losing a 150-year-old guiding star and optimism about what comes next. "But what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."

news.summary_en: Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini, which utilizes a looped transformer architecture where 12 of its 24 layers execute three times to enhance reasoning without increasing token generation. The MoE model features 26.4 billion total parameters with 5.4 billion active per token, supports a 1-million-token context window, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.
paragraphs: Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini, a so-called looped transformer. A looped transformer runs certain layers multiple times for each token. Inkling 2 Mini runs 12 of its 24 layers three times in a row. That lets the model reason internally for longer without generating more text, finding the right answer with fewer tokens, according to Thinking Machines. The open mixture-of-experts model has 26.4 billion parameters, with 5.4 billion active per token because of the loops, the company says. It processes text and images, has a 1-million-token context window, and is licensed under Apache 2.0.

Inkling 2 Mini leads all open models under 100 billion parameters on agentic coding tests, scoring 48.2 percent on DeepSWE v1.1 and 46.5 percent on the Vals Index v2.2. Artificial Analysis gives it 20 points on its Intelligence Index, tying it with Qwen3.8 27B at roughly six times lower cost and four times the speed.

Inkling 2 Mini runs locally on Macs with at least 32 GB of memory and on Nvidia's DGX Spark. You can download the weights and a research version with variable loops from Hugging Face. It is also available to try in the Tinker Playground.

news.author: Matthias Bastian
news.summary_en:
US tech stocks are tumbling. The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6 percent on Friday and dropped 10.4 percent for the week, its worst showing since the Covid-19 crisis. That leaves the index 20 percent below its October peak and in bear market territory, according to the Financial Times. paragraphs: US tech stocks are tumbling. The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6 percent on Friday and dropped 10.4 percent for the week, its worst showing since the Covid-19 crisis. That leaves the index 20 percent below its October peak and in bear market territory, according to the Financial Times. Doubts over multibillion-dollar AI buildouts, the Nvidia scandal and questionable China deals, and political headwinds after Democrats' midterm win are driving the sell-off like a perfect storm.

Investors are also debating whether high valuations for chip and memory stocks are still justified given their cyclical nature. Meanwhile, high oil costs from the Iran war are fueling persistent inflation and keeping interest rates high.

Nvidia took the hardest hit on Friday, plunging 14 percent after reports that the SEC is reviewing its accounting. The US semiconductor index also dropped 10.7 percent, with losses across memory and chip stocks including Sandisk, Micron, and Broadcom. Anthropic fell 9.1 percent a day after its market debut.

news.title: The Race to Build a Quantum Computer Has Become a Sprint
news.title_en: The Race to Build a Quantum Computer Has Become a Sprint

inline_images.caption: Hartmut Neven, a physicist heading Google’s Quantum A.I. Lab in California, where he works on a kind of quantum computing involving neutral atoms, in which individual atoms are trapped with beams of light. (Ariana Drehsler for The New York Times)

news.author: Cade Metz
news.content_snippet:
For almost a decade, a Google lab in Santa Barbara, Calif., has led the global race to build a computer that harnesses the power of quantum mechanics: the unseen physical properties that allow light, subatomic particles and other exotic matter to behave in ways that defy common sense.
