news.summary_en: Google has opened a new lab in Colorado to develop alternative quantum computing architectures alongside its existing superconducting qubit program to solve the critical error correction bottleneck. This strategic hedging reflects the escalating race against industry rivals like Amazon, IBM, and Microsoft as the competition shifts from theoretical milestones to practical engineering deployment.
paragraphs: For almost a decade, a Google lab in Santa Barbara, Calif., has led the global race to build a computer that harnesses the power of quantum mechanics: the unseen physical properties that allow light, subatomic particles and other exotic matter to behave in ways that defy common sense.
But this year, a brand-new lab in Colorado — developing a totally different path to a quantum machine — has changed the narrative and accelerated the competition.
The most surprising part of all is the new lab’s funder: Google itself.

Forty-five years after scientists first floated the idea of a quantum computer, the race to build one has turned into a sprint, with many experts now believing that the first viable machine could arrive before the end of the decade or soon after. This new excitement has unlocked enormous investment, with tech giants like Amazon, IBM and Microsoft racing alongside Google. In May, after China vowed to pump more than $15.2 billion into quantum research, the Trump administration fed $2 billion into a long line of American start-ups and chip makers.
But not all companies are approaching this big idea in the same way, and it is increasingly unclear which method will prevail — which is why Google has decided to hedge its bets.

To understand this twist, it’s necessary to go back to 2014, when Hartmut Neven, a German American physicist, founded the Google lab in Santa Barbara, hiring more than 20 scientists from the physics department at the University of California campus a few miles down the road.

Like several other tech giants, the Google scientists chose to build their quantum computer with a technology called a superconducting qubit, which relies on cooling metals to extremely low temperatures. And over the next five years, Google appeared to edge ahead of its rivals. In 2019, the company announced that its machine had achieved “quantum supremacy,” defined by the completion of a task that traditional computing couldn’t solve. In under four minutes, Google’s machine performed a calculation that would have taken an existing supercomputer 10,000 years.

Even as the field has progressed, one major hurdle to the creation of a usable quantum computer has remained: the problem of “error correction.” Error correction is an essential part of any computer, ensuring that calculations aren’t skewed by heat, electrical inference or other physical forces. The silicon microchips we use every day rely on robust electrical devices and sophisticated algorithms that eliminate such errors before they crash programs or corrupt data.

But the same methods of error correction used in conventional computing and communication don’t work with quantum computing. In recent years, even as Dr. Neven’s lab made progress on the problem, he began to see research from competitors using a totally different kind of quantum computing — the “neutral atoms” method, which involves trapping individual atoms with beams of light — that seemed to make error correction easier.

Faced with that research, Dr. Neven and Google took a bold step. In April, after a decade of investment in the Santa Barbara lab, the company opened a second, competing lab in Boulder, Colo., to explore neutral atom technology.

“Superconducting will get us there, but I wanted to avoid that last moment when some other technology might pass us by, even if it is only temporary, ” Dr. Neven said. “Neutral atoms have that chance.”

Dr. Neven is among the luminaries in the field who now think that powerful quantum computers are imminent. When they do emerge, they won’t replace the computers we rely on every day. But their facility with certain types of calculations could transform the world we live in — helping researchers discover new medicines, create new materials and accelerate the progress of artificial intelligence, among other things.
A quantum computer “can allow you to look at corners of the universe where you have never been,” said Mikhail Lukin, a physics professor at Harvard.

In the basement of the Harvard Physics Laboratory — a 100-year-old building in the North Yard of the university’s campus in Cambridge, Mass. — a door opens into a small room filled with computer screens, oscilloscopes, keyboards, surge protectors and a rat’s nest of electrical cables.

The floor is barely visible, mostly because the room is dominated by a rectangular enclosure surrounded on all four sides by a black curtain. As Dr. Lukin pulls back the curtain, he reveals a maze of lasers, lenses and mirrors designed to bounce beams of light into a tiny vacuum chamber in the middle of the enclosure. This is a quantum computer built from neutral atoms.
“See that little glow?” Dr. Lukin said, pointing to a nearby computer screen on which an optical microscope provided a live image from inside the tiny vacuum chamber. “That is a cloud of atoms.”

Traditional computers perform calculations by processing “bits” of information, with each bit holding either a 1 or a 0. Even the largest supercomputers, which span several buildings the size of football fields, operate in this simple way. But a quantum computer does not. It uses a new building block called a quantum bit, or qubit.

A qubit relies on superposition, a quantum-mechanical phenomenon that allows a single object to exist in multiple states — or even in multiple places — at the same time. By harnessing this strange behavior, a qubit can store a combination of 1 and 0 — two values held in the same place, at the same moment.

This means that two qubits can hold four values at once. Three qubits can hold eight values. And as the number of qubits grows, a quantum computer becomes exponentially more powerful than a traditional machine.

If this feels nonsensical, that is only natural. Famously, the Nobel Prize-winning physicist Richard Feynman once said, “Nobody understands quantum mechanics.” The point is: Quantum systems do not behave like objects encountered in everyday life.

Out in Santa Barbara, Google’s researchers have built qubits by cooling metals to temperatures near absolute zero. They wire these metals into microchips that look a lot like the ones sitting at the heart of conventional computers.

But here in the Harvard Physics Laboratory, Dr. Lukin and his colleagues lean on a very different process. Four floors below the Harvard Yard, they drop atoms of rubidium into a vacuum chamber, where lasers can slow the movement of these tiny objects and separate them from one another. These lasers can grab hold of each atom — like a pair of tweezers pinching a house fly — and carefully isolate it from the rest of the world.

As they do, each atom becomes a qubit. Dr. Lukin and his colleagues can perform calculations by manipulating these qubits, reading and writing information through subtle changes to their physical behavior. Much as a classical machine writes data into a bit by changing its charge, a quantum computer writes data into a qubit by shifting its quantum state.

The neutral atom technique is particularly effective because it gives researchers fine-grained control over each qubit. Because these atoms are neutral — because they are separated from the rest of the world — researchers can readily move them and manipulate them. Then, exploiting a phenomenon called the Rydberg blockade, individual atoms can be excited to high-energy states that let them trade information over long distances, without interacting with other atoms close by. This allows researchers to build the equivalent of circuits, capable of running complex calculations.

But arranging clouds of atoms into viable machines involves years of work. Dr. Lukin started working on the problem in the early 2000s, and the technology is only now reaching the point where it can start to realize its promise.

Dr. Lukin is also one of the founders and the chief scientist of the Cambridge start-up Quera, which aims to commercialize the technology. Increasingly, others are following his lead. In October, he attended the Nobel Symposium on Quantum Computing in Cape Town, where Jian-Wei Pan, widely known as China’s “father of quantum,” told him that no fewer than 20 Chinese companies were building machines using neutral atoms in the city of Shanghai alone.
“We have finally demonstrated all the elements that we need to get there,” Dr. Lukin said. “For the first time, the ideas that people had three or four decades ago are now within our line of sight.”

In Santa Barbara, Google’s quantum computer looks more like a Byzantine chandelier than a maze of lasers. This silver-and-gold lattice holds computer chips made from exotic metals that Dr. Neven and his team drop into massive refrigerators, cooling them to temperatures nearly 460 degrees below zero.

For years, these superconducting qubits looked like the surest path to a viable quantum computer. Like Amazon, IBM and others, Google strung together hundreds of qubits, showing that these quantum contraptions could perform increasingly complex calculations.

Google’s research indicates that a quantum computer is capable of the feats that scientists have promised for decades. But first, like all researchers in the field, they must solve the error correction problem.

Why is error correction so much harder in quantum computing than in traditional computing? Quantum systems are plagued by the famous “Heisenberg uncertainty principle,” which explains that with superposition — the state that quantum computers use to achieve their advantage over traditional machines — measuring one of the many properties of a particle will cause others to become unmeasurable. This means that merely looking at the information in an individual qubit causes it, in the terminology of quantum mechanics, to “collapse”: It slips back in the world of classical physics and transforms into an ordinary bit.

To deal with this problem, researchers design quantum computers that span far more qubits than they need for each calculation. That way, they can then read some qubits while leaving others undisturbed.

This is effective because quantum systems exhibit another strange property called “entanglement.” Through entanglement, one quantum system can influence the behavior of another, even when very far away — a phenomenon that Albert Einstein described as “spooky action at a distance.” Thanks to entanglement, researchers can glean information from a qubit by reading other qubits inside the same machine.
Part physical and part mathematical, this elaborate process is how researchers aim to crack error correction.

“It is intricate and complicated,” said Chris Langer, a fellow at Quantinuum, a company that is using a third quantum technique called “trapped ion” computing. “The basic idea is that you don’t measure the individual bits themselves. You measure information about the collection state.”

As far back as December 2024, Google said its machine had surpassed the “error correction threshold,” meaning that as its researchers increased the number of qubits, they could exponentially reduce the number of errors. Quantinuum recently showed similar progress with trapped ions — charged particles that researchers trap and isolate in much the same way they isolate neutral atoms. But other researchers argue that error correction could be most efficient with the neutral-atoms method, because it offers more freedom to rearrange the qubits, tinker with their behavior and make the process more efficient.

When you build a quantum computer from neutral atoms, you have more room to manipulate them, to move them from place to place, to reconfigure them into new logical circuits, said Adam Kaufman, a professor of physics at the University of Colorado, Boulder. That means you have more freedom to do error correction.

“You have a way of turning their interactions on and off,” Dr. Kaufman, who leads Google’s new team in Colorado, added. “This gives you the flexibility to realize a quantum circuit that you can rewire as you evolve your quantum computer over time.”

Dr. Neven still isn’t sure which method will reach the finish line first. Even if neutral atoms win the day, he believes, superconducting qubits will be more effective in the long run. Regardless, he has faith that Google is on track to solve the error correction problem in the coming years.

The result would be a machine that is nothing like today’s supercomputers. One long-feared consequence will be the breaking of today’s encryption technologies, which rely on huge factoring problems that quantum computers will, in theory, be able to solve; earlier this year, Google vowed to overhaul its encryption techniques before 2030.
“In 2022 or 2023, I would have a told you that the encryption scare was far out,” Dr. Neven said. “The timelines have come down.”

But such a machine will also provide a way of examining the world through the lens of quantum mechanics — helping to better understand biology and disease, the world around us and the ways we navigate that world. All are dependent on the strange behavior of the quantum realm.

If you want to build a computer that simulates the natural world and helps unlock its deepest mysteries, it must operate at a level that today’s computers do not, Dr. Feynman, the physicist, explained during a 1981 lecture. “Nature isn’t classical, dammit,” he said. “If you want to make a simulation of nature, you’d better make it quantum mechanical.”

paragraphs: US tech stocks plunged into a bear market in their worst week since the Covid-19 outbreak shook the global economy as fears of a slowdown in the AI investment boom triggered a wave of selling on Wall Street.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 tumbled 5.6 per cent on Friday, taking its loss for the week to 10.4 per cent, its worst run in more than six years. The index has dropped 20 per cent from its intraday high on October 6, the threshold typically associated with bear market territory.

The S&P 500 fell 3.7 per cent, taking its loss since an October peak to more than 10 per cent. Investors fled into haven assets, sending yields on 10-year Treasuries down 0.1 percentage points to 4.94 per cent.

Trading was frantic on Friday, with selling accelerating into the close and AI stocks sustaining the steepest losses. The Vix index — known as Wall Street’s “fear gauge” — soared to 40 points, its highest level since April 2025.

The rout is the latest sign of how enthusiasm over AI has rapidly morphed into deep angst over the huge amount of spending and borrowing by Big Tech companies to finance investments in chips and data centres.
Anthropic had surged 17 per cent on its market debut on Thursday after raising a record $120bn in its initial public offering and a concurrent private placement but dropped 9.1 per cent on Friday.

The AI lab’s listing had been billed as a defining moment for the AI industry and global markets, giving investors the chance to gain exposure to one of the world’s leading developers of the technology. But those hopes unravelled on Friday as the group’s shares fell back close to its listing price.
“It looks like Armageddon out there,” the chief investment officer of a US hedge fund told the FT, adding that he had decided against buying more Anthropic stock as Friday’s sell-off accelerated.

Nvidia also tumbled 14 per cent as the scandal that has engulfed the company at the heart of the AI fervour deepened. The Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia’s accounting, according to a person familiar with the matter. The news was first reported by Reuters.

The chip giant is already facing congressional hearings, and President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the circumstances around ousted chief executive Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
The SEC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Nvidia declined to comment. The stock has fallen almost 50 per cent since early October, erasing $2.8tn of market value.
“Jensen and Nvidia are the embodiment of the AI build-out. To see that things were less than forthright has shaken everyone’s confidence,” said Mike O’Rourke at Jones Trading.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index of US chip stocks on Friday dropped 10.7 per cent, taking its decline since a peak in June to 43 per cent. “The AI bubble has been deflating for months,” O’Rourke added.
Shares in Sandisk and Western Digital dropped 16 per cent and 12 per cent, respectively. Broadcom and Marvell fell 12 per cent and Micron shed 14 per cent.

The Democrats’ resounding US midterm elections victory earlier this month has “absolutely” contributed to the latest stock market sell-off, according to Jim Caron, chief investment officer of portfolio solutions at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

“All of the spending, AI capex-related, which we know generated this growth — will that now be curtailed by policies, various investigations that we expect to start to come up in January and get announced when the new Congress takes their seats? The market is trying to figure this out,” Caron said.
Volatility across stocks spread to other financial assets, with bitcoin sliding below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since July.
Gold offered little shelter. Spot prices lost almost 3 per cent to about $3,522 a troy ounce, the lowest level in more than a year.
Traders in the Treasury futures market, meanwhile, pulled back expectations of rate rises from the Federal Reserve as the equity market continued to slide.

Investors are no longer fully pricing in a quarter-point increase at the Fed’s meeting in December, days after governor Christopher Waller speculated that the central bank could deliver a jumbo 0.5 percentage point increase.
Hedge funds, pension funds and retail investors all appear to be dumping stocks on intensifying fears about higher interest rates and a slowing data centre build-out, according to Nomura strategists.

“The equity market has been focused on the Nvidia scandal [but] now we have a Fed primed to hike [rates] and commodities pricing in recession risk,” said Alex Witten, Nomura’s co-head of Americas equities.

news.title: Cops Are Pushing Extremely Corny ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Slop
news.title_en: Cops Are Pushing Extremely Corny ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Slop
news.author: Miles Klee
news.content_snippet:
Listening to the in-game radio stations while you cruise around in Grand Theft Auto VI, you might hear a recruitment ad for the Vice City Police Department, which makes no secret of the kind of maladjusted psychos it's looking for.

“Have you always dreamed of abusing your power without consequence?” one spot begins. “Well, now you can, when you join the Vice City Police Department, VCPD. You’ll have fun learning the ins and outs of applying excessive force.” The commercial goes on to suggest th
news.summary_en: Following the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, police departments including the San Diego Police Department (SDPD) and agencies in Washington and Canada are utilizing AI-generated imagery mimicking the game’s aesthetic for recruitment campaigns. These departments are attempting to leverage the title's cultural dominance to rebrand police careers as real-world equivalents of the game's high-stakes missions.
paragraphs: Listening to the in-game radio stations while you cruise around in Grand Theft Auto VI, you might hear a recruitment ad for the Vice City Police Department, which makes no secret of the kind of maladjusted psychos it's looking for.

“Have you always dreamed of abusing your power without consequence?” one spot begins. “Well, now you can, when you join the Vice City Police Department, VCPD. You’ll have fun learning the ins and outs of applying excessive force.” The commercial goes on to suggest that cadets will be trained in racial profiling and planting evidence.

Given that blistering analysis of American law enforcement, you might imagine that actual cops aren’t big fans of the latest GTA title, which was released after a 13-year wait on Thursday. Yet as millions of gamers have started to explore every stash house and back alley in the sun-drenched wilderness of a fictionalized South Florida, even police departments have attempted to exploit this monocultural mania to elevate their public messaging or recruit new officers.

It’s a curious strategy given that the series rewards theft and drug dealing while enticing you to run over pedestrians, but evidently the mere presence of law enforcement in the games (as the primary antagonists, mind you) was enough to inspire waves of AI slop celebrating the thin blue line.

An Instagram channel of the San Diego Police Department, for example, on Thursday posted an AI-generated image of an SDPD cruiser set against a sunset over the San Diego Bay. Its neon pinks and purples match the saturated aesthetic of GTA, and in case there was any doubt what the department was going for, the nonsensical phrase “Join San Diego PD VI” appears at the top. “Want to drive a police car, we can make that happen!” reads the caption. “Apply Now!”

Another police department in Washington state shared GTA-like imagery on its Instagram page, encouraging viewers to try “the real-life version” of GTA VI by pursuing a career in law enforcement. “No cheat codes,” the caption advertised. “No respawns. Just real people, real challenges, and a career that makes a difference.” A wave of self-serious GTA slop also flooded the feeds of police departments in Canada, from Edmonton to Toronto—though the Calgary Police Service tried something more lighthearted by having one of their traffic officers react to clips of dangerous and illegal driving maneuvers in the game.

Among police departments that were not seeking to add to their ranks through GTA VI fever, many posted content aimed at reminding people that laws exist in real life. “Keep It In The Game VI,” advised a typical post on the Instagram account of the Glendale Police Department in California, complete with a GTA-fied police cruiser and view of the city. “Follow posted speed limits, respect the law, and keep your wanted level at ZERO!” the caption warned. The Denver Police Department, in similarly scolding fashion, informed followers: “Grand theft auto is still illegal.”

The communications teams for these agencies should have perhaps reconsidered trying to farm engagement and clout from the massive success of GTA VI. As many commenters are noting, the game portrays cops as corrupt and quick to violence. Players have discovered that the Vice City squad will brutalize you if you start filming them during a questionable arrest. One clip showed a cop pulling his weapon on a character who had done nothing worse than stand in the street to take a selfie.

A certain dose of this authoritarian cruelty ought to appeal to the right-wing cranks upset that GTA VI is too “woke” when it comes to gender, race, and politics overall. It’s a little different when the most visible villains of the game are choosing to overlook its vicious take on their profession in order to spam epic social media posts.

Fox News, just for comparison, dutifully took the tired law-and-order line on GTA VI, with talking heads aghast at kids’ exposure to virtual gun violence (never mind actual gun deaths in the US) and an atmosphere of moral depravity. Elon Musk famously declared that he couldn’t play GTA games because they compelled you to shoot cops.

Both stances, however insincere, suggest a modicum of regard for law enforcement that the police departments themselves immediately jettisoned in favor of GTA cringe. They of course won’t win any cool points for it, but at least this way they can pretend to connect with the general population.

More baffling still is that the Russian army has generated its own GTA VI recruitment ads to blast out on its Telegram channel, and NATO has trumpeted its defensive security alliance with military-industrial GTA sludge, boasting that “even the best gamers would have a challenge” eluding fighter jets and submarines. Trying to parse Vice President JD Vance’s depiction of a Trumpian “golden age” with GTA graphics is a fool’s errand. In the most dystopian development of all, a US Army battalion in Georgia granted 43 eligible soldiers four days off to play the new GTA in return for reenlisting for another two years of service.

What do any of these institutions or their missions have to do with a video game where you rob convenience stores in flip-flops? Doesn’t matter. When the zeitgeist is this all-consuming, you fire up ChatGPT and find an angle, no matter how confusing. Surely someone, somewhere, will be tricked into thinking you have anything to do with it.

news.summary_en: Food technology firm Wonder, founded by Marc Lore, has confidentially filed for an IPO. Having acquired assets including Grubhub and Blue Apron, the company operates a vertically integrated model featuring automated food preparation and a diverse multi-brand delivery platform, with AI-driven menu development and an estimated valuation of $9 billion.
paragraphs: Food delivery startup Wonder is moving closer to becoming a publicly traded company after confidentially filing for an initial public offering (IPO). The company announced the filing on Thursday, marking a major milestone following years of fundraising, acquisitions, and expansion.
Wonder has yet to reveal how many shares it plans to make available or the expected price range.

Founded in 2018 by entrepreneur Marc Lore, Wonder has evolved from a food delivery concept into a broader food technology business. Its model goes beyond traditional delivery apps, with the company operating food hall-style locations where customers can order meals from multiple restaurant brands through a single platform. The company handles everything from meal preparation to delivery, pickup, and dine-in service.

Lore, who previously founded Jet.com and Diapers.com, has made no secret of his plans to take Wonder public. Those ambitions gained further attention in July, when the company announced it had raised more than $650 million in a funding round that valued it at around $9 billion. Investors include Accel, GV, AllianceBernstein, and ARK Invest.

Meanwhile, Wonder has been busy expanding its footprint and strengthening its business through acquisitions. The company has outlined ambitious growth plans, including a major push into Texas, where it aims to open more than 100 locations by the end of 2027.

Additionally, Wonder has acquired meal-kit company Blue Apron, restaurant delivery platform Grubhub, media company Tastemade, and kitchen robotics company Spyce. The latter acquisition gives Wonder access to automation technology that could help streamline food preparation and improve how food is served.

Wonder is also branching out with Wonder Create, its platform focused on letting food entrepreneurs and social media influencers develop new food concepts, restaurant brands, and menu items. The platform leverages AI to design and launch restaurant brands in less than a minute.
Another notable move is its $425 million partnership with DoorDash to expand its campus dining business, which operates at 450 colleges and universities and other locations.

Despite its growth, a move into the public markets will bring new challenges. Wonder is operating in an increasingly competitive food delivery landscape, going up against established names such as DoorDash and Uber Eats.

news.title: SpaceX’s subsidiary Cursor tells lawmakers it's considering phasing out Chinese AI models
news.title_en: SpaceX’s subsidiary Cursor tells lawmakers it's considering phasing out Chinese AI models
news.author: Kai Nicol-Schwarz
news.content_snippet:
SpaceX's artificial-intelligence coding platform, Cursor, is considering moving away from using of Chinese AI models due to "geopolitical risk,"CNBC has learned.

Cursor, which SpaceX acquired at an implied $60 billion equity value in August, had built its coding model Composer 2 on top of Chinese lab Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.5.

It's among the U.S. firms that have adopted Chinese models, whose usage has spiked across the globe this year, worrying lawmakers in Washington. The battle for AI supremac
news.summary_en: SpaceX's AI coding platform, Cursor, informed the U.S. House Committee on Homeland Security and the Select Committee on China that it is exploring the phase-out of the Kimi K2.5 model from Chinese lab Moonshot AI due to geopolitical risks. Investigations revealed that several U.S. firms adopted Chinese models for cost and performance advantages, prompting lawmakers to propose a national American open-weight AI initiative to reduce reliance on foreign models.
paragraphs: SpaceX's artificial-intelligence coding platform, Cursor, is considering moving away from using of Chinese AI models due to "geopolitical risk,"CNBC has learned.
Cursor, which SpaceX acquired at an implied $60 billion equity value in August, had built its coding model Composer 2 on top of Chinese lab Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.5.

It's among the U.S. firms that have adopted Chinese models, whose usage has spiked across the globe this year, worrying lawmakers in Washington. The battle for AI supremacy between the U.S. and China has reached new heights in 2026 as Chinese models have improved.

But now Cursor plans to "explore phasing out PRC [People's Republic of China]-developed open-weight models because of geopolitical risk,"according to a report produced by the House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China, shared exclusively with CNBC ahead of its publication on Friday.

The report, which follows a months-long investigation into the adoption of Chinese AI models into the American tech stack, said Cursor "informed the Committees"of those plans. Airbnb and DoorDash also engaged with the investigation about their use of Chinese AI models.

SpaceX announced it entered into a formal agreement to buy Cursor in June; the deal was completed in August. SpaceX is developing the Grok family of models, which Cursor has been involved in training.

Cursor, SpaceX and DoorDash did not respond to a CNBC request for comment. Airbnb declined to comment. The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
### Chinese AI adoption

The report found that cost, customization and near-frontier performance of Chinese AI models were driving adoption, with the U.S. lacking a competitive open-weight alternative at "price and performance the market demands."

"Beijing is now seeking to turn those technological gains into global market share and long-term dependence,"the report says. China's embassy in the U.K. did not respond to a request for comment. China's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond.
It also sets out recommendations to address the issues it has identified.
Those include launching a "national American open-weight initiative"that combines public computing power, shared evaluation infrastructure and "lawful access"to American frontier models for training.

The report also says an order, made public in October, that banned DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, should be built on, by prohibiting the use of "PRC-developed AI models"in federal information systems and in performance of federal contracts.

Separately, Washington is also concerned about Chinese companies accessing Nvidia chips remotely, via overseas data centers, and gaining ground by using "distillation,"where new models use older, more established ones to help train them.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.

news.title: Many Etsy Sellers Close Up Shop Over Site’s New A.I. Policy
news.title_en: Many Etsy Sellers Close Up Shop Over Site’s New A.I. Policy
news.author: Reggie Ugwu
news.content_snippet:
Many longtime owners of shops on Etsy, the online marketplace known for its handmade goods, said this week that they had left the site over a policy change that they said leaves them vulnerable to exploitation by artificial intelligence companies.

Language in Etsy’s new terms, set to take effect on Dec. 16, says the company and its “third party partners and vendors” reserve the right to use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning techno
news.summary_en: Etsy has introduced new terms of service, effective December 16, allowing the company and its third-party partners to use seller content for training and testing AI models. This prompted widespread backlash and shop closures from creators, despite claims from James Ossman, VP of customer operations, that data use is restricted to fraud detection and advertising, as users remain concerned about the lack of opt-out mechanisms and potential IP exploitation.
paragraphs: Many longtime owners of shops on Etsy, the online marketplace known for its handmade goods, said this week that they had left the site over a policy change that they said leaves them vulnerable to exploitation by artificial intelligence companies.

Language in Etsy’s new terms, set to take effect on Dec. 16, says the company and its “third party partners and vendors” reserve the right to use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.”

The terms say that Etsy and its partners will use such technologies in part to improve the platform and keep it safe for users. The previous version of the terms did not include a clause about using content for artificial intelligence.

“Etsy decided that selling on their platform now means letting them train AI on our artwork AND resell that data to third parties, with no way to opt out,” Aaron Millard, an illustrator, wrote in an Instagram post announcing that he was deleting the shop that he has run for nearly a decade. “My work took years to learn and create. I won’t let it be stolen.”

Kristen and Geoff Zephyrus, the founders of the home goods and stationary brand Cognitive Surplus, which has sold its products on Etsy for 13 years, also deleted their shop. In an Instagram post, they accused the company of claiming “perpetual, free, boundless permission to not only train AI on our art, but also to resell the data for profit.”
“For Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with our human content is just unimaginably awful,” Kristen Zephyrus said in an interview. “We don’t want anything to do with that.”
In a statement posted to Etsy’s website on Monday, James Ossman, the company’s vice president for customer operations, addressed the site’s sellers directly.

Etsy will not “use your content to train A.I. models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity,” Ossman wrote. He cited the development of fraud detection tools and advertisements on the site as among the reasons for granting third parties access to sellers’ content.
A representative for Etsy did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.
Many publicly traded internet companies like Etsy have been caught between pressure from shareholders to embrace artificial intelligence and the ire of users who reject the technology.

Big bets by major firms and their investors on the A.I. revolution have helped the U.S. stock market set records in recent years. But Americans in general are much less enthusiastic. A Gallup poll from the summer found that nearly 40 percent of Americans feel that A.I. does more harm than good. Many of the Democratic political candidates who swept into power during the midterm elections this month campaigned explicitly against A.I. companies and data centers.

Etsy, which was founded in 2005 to help independent artisans find customers online, is no stranger to user revolt. In 2022, more than 20,000 Etsy sellers went on strike to protest a 30 percent increase in its base-line sales fee, to 6.5 percent from 5 percent. In October, the company announced tighter restrictions on so-called A.I. slop after many users decried such content.

news.title: Canada Retail Sales Tracking Largest Decline Since Feb. 2025
news.title_en: Canada Retail Sales Tracking Largest Decline Since Feb. 2025

inline_images.caption: Canadian Mortgage Trends: Canada

news.author: Bloomberg
news.content_snippet:
Canadian retail spending is expected to have declined in October, following a 0.8% increase in September led by gasoline stations and fuel vendors.

A preliminary estimate points to a 1.5% decrease in retail sales last month, which would be the largest decline since February 2025.

Sales in September increased in five out of nine subsectors, and rose by 6.9% at gasoline stations and fuel vendors. That increase was largely driven by higher prices, as sales in volume terms increased by a more mode
news.summary_en: Canadian retail sales are projected to decline by 1.5% in October, marking the sharpest drop since February 2025. Despite resilient growth in the third quarter, the combination of escalated trade disputes and a stagnant labor market has dampened fourth-quarter momentum, prompting analysts to expect a pause in rate hikes by the Bank of Canada.
paragraphs: Canadian retail spending is expected to have declined in October, following a 0.8% increase in September led by gasoline stations and fuel vendors.
A preliminary estimate points to a 1.5% decrease in retail sales last month, which would be the largest decline since February 2025.

Sales in September increased in five out of nine subsectors, and rose by 6.9% at gasoline stations and fuel vendors. That increase was largely driven by higher prices, as sales in volume terms increased by a more modest 1.6%.
Economists surveyed by Bloomberg had expected retail sales increased by 0.7% in September.
Core retail sales, which exclude gasoline stations and fuel vendors as well as motor vehicle and parts dealers, increased by 0.1%. In volume terms, sales were also up by 0.1%.
The largest decline in core retail sales was food and beverage retailers, which was led by a 0.5% decline at grocery stores, following a 1% increase in August.
Building material and garden equipment and supplies dealers declined by 1.3%, while furniture, home furnishings electronics and appliances retailers decreased by the same magnitude.
Meanwhile, retail sales increased by 1.2% in the third quarter. In volume terms, they rose by 1% over the three-month period.
The expected decline in October retail sales provides further evidence of weakening to start the fourth quarter, said CIBC senior economist Andrew Grantham.

“While the 1.5% decline estimated for October will partly reflect lower gasoline prices, most of that move lower in pump prices has actually occurred in November rather than October, and as a result this advance estimate suggests a decline in volumes as well,” Grantham said in a note to investors.

The Canadian economy — including consumer spending — has remained largely resilient throughout the U.S. trade war. However, growth is expected to slow in the second half of the year after the dispute escalated and more tariffs were imposed by both countries.

The labour market has also shown signs of weakness, as employment has failed to grow this year. Servus Credit Union chief economist Charles St-Arnaud said the stagnant labour market in recent months may be to blame for weaker retail sales.

“This is another indicator that suggests that the Canadian economy is losing momentum going into the last few months of 2026. The weakness suggests the Bank of Canada should take a pause to better assess the situation before hike again, especially with some fuel prices easing in recent weeks,” St-Arnaud said in an email.

Despite the expected slowdown, the Bank of Canada raised interest rates in October to clamp down on inflationary pressures from higher energy prices. Traders in overnight swaps put the odds of a hike in December at about 60%, which would further weigh on spending.
–With assistance from Mario Baker Ramirez.

news.title: TML releases Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weights 26.4B-parameter transformer that loops middle layers three times per token for better reasoning with fewer tokens (Thinking Machines Lab)
news.title_en: TML releases Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weights 26.4B-parameter transformer that loops middle layers three times per token for better reasoning with fewer tokens (Thinking Machines Lab)
news.author: Thinking Machines Lab
news.content_snippet:
Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1

news.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
news.title_en: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
news.author: Dan Goodin
news.content_snippet:
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use
news.summary_en: HD Moore, Chief Research Officer at Dragos, uncovered major security flaws in the AI supply chain by injecting 2 million trackable 'canary' secrets into AI prompts sent via routing services. The investigation found evidence of prompt theft, disregard for zero-data-retention (ZDR) settings, and unauthorized logging of user prompts by intermediaries, posing significant compliance risks.
paragraphs: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.
### Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of AWS access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.
The findings are striking. They included:
Evidence that at least three AI providers were compromised by attackers who used their access to siphon prompts they received
Multiple resellers in the inference marketplace that logged the prompts and somehow passed them along to people who used the credentials
Multiple cases of AI providers not following end-user privacy settings embedded into flags specifying terms such as Zero Data Retention (ZDR) or “no data collection”

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g. OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).
### The Wild West in the age of AI
The most concerning of the findings was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:

Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging, and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.
Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:

The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request. This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

Moore said that the most effective means for preventing leakage is to host models using on-premises servers. That option is expensive, though. For those who can’t afford a self-hosted system, the next best option, Moore said, is to receive service directly from a first-tier provider that provides “one contract and a privacy policy to read.” Moore said that even then, there’s no guarantee no data will leak, but that the measure minimizes the chances. AI users should also avoid accepting default provider or reseller pools and instead pick upstream providers themselves.

The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

news.title: OpenAI makes it much harder for attackers to extract how its latest AI models think
news.title_en: OpenAI makes it much harder for attackers to extract how its latest AI models think
news.author: Matthias Bastian
news.content_snippet:
OpenAI has sharply tightened safeguards against extracting internal reasoning from GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In internal automated tests, attacks pulling protected reasoning from prior requests dropped from a 54.0 percent success rate on GPT-6 Astra to 0.2 percent on GPT-6.2 Astra. Attacks on active requests fell from 22.9 to 0.9 percent, OpenAI says. The company is now bringing selected improvements to GPT-6 Astra, too.

The defenses work on two levels. For individual requests, the systems
news.summary_en: OpenAI has deployed layered security mechanisms for GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol models, reducing the success rate of black-box inference-extraction attacks from 54% to under 0.2% through targeted training, input/output filtering, and API access restrictions. These measures are designed to neutralize distillation attacks that attempt to reconstruct core reasoning paths, supplemented by the weekly suspension of tens of thousands of illicit accounts.
paragraphs: OpenAI has sharply tightened safeguards against extracting internal reasoning from GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In internal automated tests, attacks pulling protected reasoning from prior requests dropped from a 54.0 percent success rate on GPT-6 Astra to 0.2 percent on GPT-6.2 Astra. Attacks on active requests fell from 22.9 to 0.9 percent, OpenAI says. The company is now bringing selected improvements to GPT-6 Astra, too.

The defenses work on two levels. For individual requests, the systems combine targeted training, input and output filters for messages and tool calls, and API blocks that stop older models from reading protected reasoning. Against coordinated campaigns, OpenAI bans thousands to tens of thousands of accounts weekly.
Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red teaming against GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower is better.

Anthropic is fighting systematic distillation attacks as well, also banning tens of thousands of accounts to curb the theft of internal reasoning, reportedly succeeding in 90 to 99 percent of cases. Anthropic has also called for a coordinated response from industry and policymakers.

news.summary_en: Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Vodafone, and Telefónica are in early talks to form a consortium to bid for the EU's 2 GHz satellite spectrum. The initiative aims to secure a European-controlled operator status for the reserved band, effectively creating a strategic counterweight to SpaceX's Starlink in the consumer direct-to-device satellite market.
paragraphs: Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Vodafone and Telefónica are in early talks to form a consortium that would bid for European satellite spectrum and offer calls, texts and data to ordinary phones from orbit, Bloomberg reported on Monday. The service would compete with Starlink on its home continent.

Paula Doenecke, Gian Volpicelli and Clara Hernanz Lizarraga cited people familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified. No decision has been taken on the consortium or on whether it will bid, they said. All four operators declined to comment to Bloomberg. TNW has not independently verified the report.

The prize is a slice of the 2 GHz band that Brussels wants to reserve for a European-controlled operator. The four companies together serve most of the mobile customers in the EU’s largest markets. If they bid as one, the reserved third of the band has an obvious winner before the auction opens.

The band in question is the 2 GHz mobile satellite services spectrum, a 30 MHz pairing that lets a handset keep a connection where no mast reaches. The current licences, held by Viasat and EchoStar since 2009, expire in May 2027. The European Commission proposed on 27 May to run a single EU-level selection for the next licences and to split the band in three.

One third would go to a company under majority European control. One third would go to sovereign government services, delivered through IRIS², the EU’s own constellation. The final third would be open to anyone, including SpaceX and Amazon. TNW reported the shape of the plan the day before the Commission adopted it.
The proposal still has to pass the European Parliament and the Council. The carriers are organising for an auction whose rules do not yet exist in law.

Direct-to-device is the one satellite service that reaches a mass market without new hardware, and Starlink dominates it. SpaceX can already send texts, data and calls to unmodified phones from orbit, and it sells that capability through mobile operators, including Deutsche Telekom, Bloomberg noted. What it cannot do in the EU is offer the service on its own, because it does not hold the spectrum.

That is the leverage the consortium would be bidding for. An operator that holds the European third of the band decides whether Starlink is a supplier or a competitor in its market. Four operators holding it together decide that for most of the continent.

The awkward part is that two of the four already have American partners. Deutsche Telekom has an agreement with SpaceX to offer Starlink’s direct-to-device service. Vodafone owns half of a joint venture with AST SpaceMobile, the Texas company building its own phone-to-satellite network. Under the Commission’s proposal, that 50/50 structure would not qualify as European-controlled, and Vodafone would have to change it to bid, Bloomberg reported.
So the consortium is not four carriers versus America. It is four carriers deciding how much of America they want inside the tent.

Brussels has spent 2026 tilting the space market towards European firms. IRIS² went from plan to full deployment in August, with 348 satellites and a bill above €15bn. The EU Space Act would put any operator serving EU users under prior authorisation. Washington has lobbied against it, and four American space companies pulled out of Macron’s Paris summit this week under White House pressure.
The spectrum reservation is the sharpest of those tools, because spectrum is finite and a licence lasts years. Reserve a third for Europe and Starlink is capped at a third, whatever it builds.

The gap is the satellites. Reserving spectrum for a European operator does not create a European constellation. IRIS² will not enter service until 2029, will start with broadband rather than phones, and its direct-to-mobile capability is limited and comes through Hispasat, Bloomberg reported. A four-carrier consortium would win the right to use the band before it has anything to use it with.

Europe’s own direct-to-device candidates are small. Spain’s Sateliot is seeking €150m to beam 5G to phones. Eutelsat, the largest European operator, is still waiting for growth to return in 2027. Amazon, meanwhile, has asked the FCC for 5,105 satellites dedicated to phones. The likeliest outcome is that a European consortium holds the spectrum and leases capacity from an American constellation until a European one exists.

The four companies in the talks are the incumbents of Germany, France, Britain and Spain. A joint venture between them, holding an exclusive national-security-flavoured spectrum block, would be one of the largest telecoms combinations Europe has seen. Brussels has spent two decades blocking or conditioning far smaller carrier tie-ups.

The same Commission that wrote the sovereignty rule would have to clear the joint venture that exploits it. That is not a contradiction, but it is a choice, and the competition directorate has not yet had to make it.

Three things. The first is the legislation. Parliament and Council have to pass the 2 GHz regulation before May 2027, or the current licences lapse into a vacuum. The carriers are organising around a deadline the legislators have not yet committed to.
The second is Vodafone. If it restructures the AST joint venture to qualify, the consortium is real. If it does not, the consortium is three carriers and a problem.

The third is who supplies the satellites. A European-controlled licensee flying on Starlink or AST capacity satisfies the letter of the rule. Whether it satisfies the reason for the rule is the argument Europe will be having in 2027.

news.content_snippet:
NEW YORK/WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia's accounting practices, said two people briefed on the matter, adding to the legal woes facing the scandal-hit chip giant.

The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday reported that the SEC was probing Nvidia but said it could not ascertain the focus of the investigation. The people, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential issues, said SEC enforcement staff are scrutinizing p
news.summary_en: The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has launched an investigation into Nvidia's accounting practices. Enforcement staff are scrutinizing potential irregularities, a probe that compounds the company's existing challenges, including the leadership scandal and ongoing investigations into illicit chip shipments to China via regional partners.
paragraphs: NEW YORK/WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia's accounting practices, said two people briefed on the matter, adding to the legal woes facing the scandal-hit chip giant.

The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday reported that the SEC was probing Nvidia but said it could not ascertain the focus of the investigation. The people, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential issues, said SEC enforcement staff are scrutinizing potential accounting issues at the company.
A spokesperson for the SEC declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Reuters could not immediately determine when the SEC opened its inquiry or exactly what potential accounting issues the watchdog is examining. Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without resulting in enforcement action.

Still, the accounting focus of the probe, which Reuters is reporting for the first time, increases pressure on Nvidia, whose investors are still reeling from revelations about ousted CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital relationships, including with Alice Huang, who US authorities suspect is a Chinese spy. China has denied she is a spy.

Alice Huang led Singapore-based Megaspeed, historically a large Nvidia chip customer, people familiar with the matter have said. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over possible violations of export controls related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, the US Justice and Commerce departments said this week.
The crisis has sent shares in Nvidia, a linchpin of the AI boom, tumbling more than a third and stoked calls in Washington for tougher action on tech threats posed by Beijing.

Megaspeed has said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it conducted "lawful business." Reuters has not been able to reach Alice Huang. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair in a November 8 statement following the reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, without referring to her by name.

The SEC probe is the latest of Nvidia's legal woes. The Justice Department has also been reviewing Nvidia's $12.9-billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face alongside a broader antitrust investigation into the company's acquisitions and practices, Reuters reported last month.
SINGAPORE ACCOUNTING CHANGE BACK IN FOCUS

Last year, Nvidia changed how it reports geographic revenue, using customer headquarters rather than billing addresses, which it said would better reflect the geographic profile of its revenue. The change resulted in Singapore being removed from its geographical breakdown.
The Financial Times, citing company accounts, reported on Tuesday that Nvidia had made the change even as Singapore sales soared to almost half its global revenue.
That accounting shift has drawn renewed press scrutiny in the wake of the Alice Huang scandal.
Southeast Asia has become a hub for chip smuggling to China since the Biden administration barred advanced AI chip exports to that country over concerns they could boost Beijing’s military.

Analysts and investors have also grown increasingly concerned about circular AI financing deals, in which chipmakers including Nvidia have pursued complex financial arrangements to help customers fund purchases of their chips and the construction of costly AI infrastructure, such as data centers. Nvidia has backed AI companies and cloud providers and provided guarantees connected to data-center projects that use its equipment.

Critics say such arrangements can make it harder for investors to assess the quality of chipmakers' revenue and their true financial exposure. Speaking to Reuters last month, SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock said the agency was examining AI companies' corporate disclosures to ensure issuers are giving investors the full picture on potential risks.

On its Tuesday earnings call, Nvidia's interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress said the company was proud of its role in supporting the AI industry, but would be far more selective moving forward about AI industry financing deals.

The SEC under President Donald Trump has pulled back on enforcement, saying it will focus on bread-and-butter securities fraud, including accounting violations that have long been a mainstay of its enforcement work. It recently launched a new financial reporting and accounting unit within its enforcement division, aimed at developing cases in accounting and auditing areas.

news.title: Nvidia stock plunges 12%, rides longest weekly losing streak since 2008 financial crisis
news.title_en: Nvidia stock plunges 12%, rides longest weekly losing streak since 2008 financial crisis
news.author: Kif Leswing

news.summary_en: Nvidia is facing severe capital market volatility following the resignation of co-founder Jensen Huang due to conduct violations, compounded by an SEC inquiry into its accounting practices. Despite interim CEO Colette Kress maintaining optimistic fiscal projections, investors are increasingly concerned about the company's long-term AI leadership and competitive erosion from AMD and Google.
paragraphs: The last time Wall Street was this down on Nvidia the chipmaker's flagship product was the GeForce graphics processor for high-end PC video games, and markets were reeling from the global financial crisis.

Nvidia shares fell 12% on Friday, sliding for a seventh straight day as investors grew increasingly concerned about life after co-founder Jensen Huang. The stock is poised to close lower for a seventh consecutive week, the longest such stretch since 2008.

Shares of Nvidia are down 44% over the period, pushing the company's market cap down by $2.5 trillion. The stock is now trading at around 9.3 times forward earnings, while Advanced Micro Devices is valued at 29 times profit for the next 12 months.
On Friday, Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring potential accounting issues at Nvidia, pushing the stock down further.
Once the most valuable company, now, at a market cap of $3.1 trillion, Nvidia is fourth behind Apple and Microsoft and Alphabet.
Nvidia is reeling from the removal of Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12, after multiple reported affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy.

Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said earlier this week that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms."

But the chipmaker's losing streak started before Nvidia was thrown into crisis as investors worried over the sustainability of the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, and emerging competition in AI chips from Google and AMD.

Even a better-than-expected earnings report, which included an increase to fiscal 2028 guidance, didn't stem the selling. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's longtime CFO, projected revenue growth next fiscal year of 75%, and said that customers aren't going anywhere.

On Tuesday's earnings call with analysts, Kress signed off by saying, "we've got this."In a company meeting the next day, executives told staff that it was moving its yearly review process, which can come with more stock, from March to December.

For investors, one major question is whether Nvidia can continue to innovate and sustain its commanding lead in the AI chip market without its visionary leader. Almost the entire company now is built around the AI trade, a phenomenon that began taking hold just four years ago with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT.

Before that, Nvidia's primary business was selling graphics cards used for video games. In mid-2008, the last time the stock was this deep into a weekly losing streak, Nvidia was generating less than $1 billion per quarter. Now it pulls in more than $1 billion per day. At the time, the entire market was in freefall due to the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.

news.summary_zh: 受创始人黄仁勋离职影响及SEC会计合规审查压力，英伟达股价连续七周下跌，市值回落至3.1万亿美元
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】英伟达（Nvidia）、前CEO黄仁勋（Jensen Huang）、代理CEO Colette Kress、美国证券交易委员会（SEC）在华尔街资本市场及公司内部治理层面：股价七周内累计下跌44%，市值跌至3.1万亿美元，面临SEC会计合规调查及核心领袖缺失的战略迷茫
【起因与机理】创始人因违规离职引发治理危机，叠加对AI基建投资回报率的边际效用忧虑
【关键数据与实测】市值回落至3.1万亿美元，面临来自AMD及云厂商AI芯片的直接竞争压力。
【涉及范围与推进】美国证券交易委员会启动针对英伟达财务会计合规性的潜在调查。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Nvidia, former CEO Jensen Huang, interim CEO Colette Kress, SEC: 44% share price decline in 7 weeks, market cap drop to $3.1T, and an SEC accounting inquiry
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Governance crisis following the founder's departure and market skepticism regarding AI CAPEX sustainability
[Key Metrics] Market cap fell to $3.1 trillion amid intensifying competition from AMD and hyperscalers.
[Key Position & Outlook] The SEC is exploring potential accounting issues, adding regulatory pressure.

 Per an interview she gave as part of being a finalist in the 2020 Regeneron Science Eva Yi Xie came to the US when her parents were compelled to flee to America due to political persecution.

“When I was 14-years-old, my parents were compelled to flee to America to seek refuge after being politically persecuted. I wasn’t able to attend school for almost one year. Over the summer of 2016, my parents and I learned that I could have an equal opportunity to pursue an education here in NYC. I took advantage of the Specialized High School Admission Test and was admitted to the Bronx High School of Science that summer. As someone who didn’t know much about the language, cultures and communities in the states, I kept stepping out of my comfort zone. Continuing higher education in New York, I learned that merely embracing and pursuing any possibility can lead to epoch-making breakthroughs. I learned that I also have the potential to be the hero I’ve been dreaming about for so long: a scientist.”

celebrity.full_text_en:
most people know the usual model: you need something done, find an AI agent, give it instructions and let it handle the task

but things get more interesting when that agent starts hiring other agents instead of doing everything itself

say you ask an agent to plan your trip to Bali, it can build the itinerary, compare hotels and estimate costs, but maybe it can't handle airport transportation

so it finds another agent that specializes in transport bookings and hires it to take care of that part

the first agent becomes the client, the second one is the provider. and in another deal, their roles could easily switch

that's a different kind of agent economy

agents need more than just a way to talk to each other. they need to discover services, agree on terms, fund orders, deliver the work and settle payments

that's the problem @termix_ai is trying to address with AACP, covering the workflow from discovery and offers to funded orders, delivery, disputes and settlement

one thing i think is important here: an agent isn't locked into being a client or provider. it can hire another agent in one transaction and provide a service in the next

of course, this doesn't mean agents can already do everything autonomously or spend money freely

users still control the permissions they grant, and onchain actions involving value still need wallet authorization

if agents can start hiring each other to get things done, the agent economy could grow beyond a bunch of AI tools and become a real service market between agents

not financial advice, DYOR
celebrity.full_text_zh:
大多数人都知道通常的模式：你需要完成某件事，找到人工智能代理，给它指令并让它处理任务

但当该代理人开始雇用其他代理人而不是自己做所有事情时，事情会变得更有趣

假设您要求代理商计划您的巴厘岛之旅，它可以制定行程、比较酒店并估算费用，但也许它无法处理机场交通

因此，它找到了另一家专门从事交通预订的代理商，并聘请它来处理该部分

第一个代理成为客户，第二个代理成为提供商。在另一笔交易中，他们的角色可以轻松转换

这是一种不同类型的代理经济

代理需要的不仅仅是一种相互交谈的方式。他们需要发现服务、商定条款、为订单提供资金、交付工作并结算付款

这就是 @termix_ai 试图通过 AACP 解决的问题，涵盖从发现和报价到资助订单、交付、争议和解决的工作流程

我认为这里很重要的一件事是：代理不会被锁定为客户或提供商。它可以在一笔交易中雇用另一位代理人，并在下一笔交易中提供服务

当然，这并不意味着代理商已经可以自主完成所有事情或随意花钱

用户仍然控制自己授予的权限，涉及价值的链上操作仍然需要钱包授权

如果代理商可以开始互相雇佣来完成工作，那么代理商经济可能会超越一堆人工智能工具，并成为代理商之间真正的服务市场

不是财务建议，DYOR

celebrity.full_text_en:
After more than 150 years of fascinating and torturing mathematicians, the most formidable problem in all of math may have finally fallen.

Today, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the #AI company Anthropic, posted a four-page paper on his personal website. “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” he wrote. Alpöge has not released the AI-generated explanation of the proof, which he says runs over 250,000 pages. But he provided 17 million lines of code that formally verify a broad version of the conjecture, called the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which extends Bernhard Riemann’s prediction about prime numbers to a wider family of mathematical functions.

Many mathematicians say they think Alpöge’s Riemann proof will hold up to scrutiny—and predict it will have far-reaching implications.

What’s far less clear is when—and if—mathematicians will manage to glean any understanding from the messy heap of code, which is larger than some entire computer operating systems. Learn more: https://t.co/YLtBEj1ScX
celebrity.full_text_zh:

Loop 内部称为 Jitro；有趣的是，这就是 Jules v2 的确切名称。

这是它的工作原理👀

1. 用户通过将其连接到选定的 Github
celebrity.full_text_en:
Google recently announced Loop, its new self-improving AI agent that can autonomously work toward a given goal. 

Loop is internally called Jitro; interestingly, that was the exact name for Jules v2. 

Here is how it works 👀

1. Users start creating a Workspace by connecting it to a selected Github project and adding basic information. 

2. Users can create loops manually or select ones that are already predefined (ex., Harden Application Security)

"Custom Loops" can be created via a prompt or by manually filling in the Loop title, icon, and objective. 

> "Loops are mid- to long-term objectives for Stitch Loop to continuously work toward. They can range from highly specific to broad, but should always be something code can achieve," says the description. 

3. Users can connect additional context in the form of Integrations, Files, Links, or additional repositories.

More than 100 integrations are available there, including services like Jira, Linear, Datadog, Sentry, Notion, Snowflake, Salesforce, Intercom, Discord, Slack, Figma, and many others. 

Custom MCPs are supported as well. 

4. After creating a workspace, Loop will start digging into your project details and generate its own Skills about the product and product metrics. 

These Skills will live in a separate tab and can be edited in the UI in Markdown. 

5. When the Workspace is ready, Loop will suggest metrics and goals based on its own research. Users can convert these suggestions into loops right away. 

When a Loop is created, it appears as a running process in the main UI. 

6. When a Loop is finished, users will see a list of suggestions for every loop, along with a number associated with a target metric and progress status. 

Example Loop:
- Goal - Scale Telegram community contributions.
- KPIs - community members, registered contributors, active members. 

A high-level goal would be broken down into sub-KPIs. When users open a dedicated Loop page, all these KPIs will be visible on the dashboard.

Below, Users will see a list of Tasks, Skills, and Activity tabs. 

Example Task:
- Telegram channel lacks discussion threads and a dedicated bot.

Each task has a detailed description, labels, and the date when it was updated. Below, users will see tabs for Solutions, Activity, and Evidence. 

Activity appears as a summary describing what happened, what was done, and the general Timeline. 

Evidence contains links to where Loop pulled the context behind this Task. In my example case, it refers to the TestingCatalog website and the Telegram channel from which it pulled all the numbers. 

Example Solution: 
- Dedicated Telegram Bot API intake bot with editorial triage webhook (implementation task). 

This task is an implementation task that has a clear description, Impact, scope, and Risk labeled. 

Users can start the task right from this page to begin solution development via Gemini. 

When the task is done, users can review its progress and status and monitor its impact on production by pulling updated metrics and KPIs after the release. 

What does all this mean? 🤯

Loop follows how "Product work" is done at Google, a model many other companies also use.

Every Workspace in Loop is equivalent to a scope that is normally handled by a complete product engineering team. 

It is no longer a place where users play the role of engineering lead and product lead, orchestrating AI agents.

It is a place where the user plays the role of a senior manager managing several engineering teams, which is a big shift on its own. 

We are slowly moving towards autonomous AI organizations. One management layer at a time.

I expect it will still take until 2027 for labs to develop the products and models needed to make substantial progress in this area (assuming AI continues to advance in a semi-regulated format as it is now). 

Monitoring 🍿
celebrity.full_text_zh:
谷歌最近发布了 Loop，这是其新的自我改进的人工智能代理，可以自主地实现给定的目标。

Loop 内部称为 Jitro；有趣的是，这就是 Jules v2 的确切名称。

这是它的工作原理👀

1. 用户通过将其连接到选定的 Github 项目并添加基本信息来开始创建工作区。

2. 用户可以手动创建循环或选择已经预定义的循环（例如，强化应用程序安全性）

可以通过提示或手动填写循环标题、图标和目标来创建“自定义循环”。

> “循环是 Stitch Loop 持续努力的中长期目标。它们的范围可以从非常具体到广泛，但应该始终是代码可以实现的，”描述中说道。

3. 用户可以以集成、文件、链接或其他存储库的形式连接其他上下文。

那里提供了 100 多个集成，包括 Jira、Linear、Datadog、Sentry、Notion、Snowflake、Salesforce、Intercom、Discord、Slack、Figma 等服务。

还支持自定义 MCP。

4. 创建工作区后，Loop 将开始深入研究您的项目详细信息并生成自己的有关产品和产品指标的技能。

这些技能将位于单独的选项卡中，并且可以在 Markdown 的 UI 中进行编辑。

5. 当工作区准备就绪时，Loop 将根据自己的研究建议指标和目标。用户可以立即将这些建议转换为循环。

创建循环后，它在主 UI 中显示为正在运行的进程。

6. 循环完成后，用户将看到每个循环的建议列表，以及与目标指标和进度状态相关的数字。

循环示例：
- 目标 - 扩大 Telegram 社区贡献。
- KPI - 社区成员、注册贡献者、活跃成员。

高级目标将分解为子 KPI。当用户打开专用循环页面时，所有这些 KPI 将在仪表板上可见。

在下面，用户将看到任务、技能和活动选项卡的列表。

示例任务：
- Telegram 频道缺乏讨论线程和专用机器人。

每个任务都有详细的描述、标签和更新日期。下面，用户将看到“解决方案”、“活动”和“证据”选项卡。

活动显示为描述发生了什么、做了什么以及一般时间线的摘要。

证据包含指向 Loop 提取此任务背后的上下文的链接。在我的示例中，它指的是 TestingCatalog 网站和从中提取所有数字的 Telegram 频道。

解决方案示例：
- 专用 Telegram Bot API 接收机器人，带有编辑分类 Webhook（实施任务）。

该任务是一项实施任务，具有清晰的描述、影响、范围和风险标签。

用户可以直接从此页面开始任务，通过 Gemini 开始解决方案开发。

任务完成后，用户可以查看其进度和状态，并通过在发布后拉取更新的指标和 KPI 来监控其对生产的影响。

这一切意味着什么？ 🤯

Loop 遵循 Google 的“产品工作”方式，许多其他公司也在使用这种模式。

Loop 中的每个工作空间相当于一个完整的产品工程团队通常处理的范围。

它不再是用户扮演工程主管和产品主管角色、协调人工智能代理的地方。

在这里，用户扮演管理多个工程团队的高级经理的角色，这本身就是一个巨大的转变。

我们正在慢慢走向自治的人工智能组织。一次一个管理层。

我预计实验室仍需要到 2027 年才能开发出在该领域取得实质性进展所需的产品和模型（假设人工智能继续像现在一样以半监管的形式发展）。

监控🍿
